summary.title: Spontaneous crystal fluctuation in hydrocarbon polymer-coated monolayer MoS 2 , MoSe 2 , WS 2 , and WSe 2 with strong photoluminescence enhancement
summary.authors: Takahiro Nakahara; Takashi Kobayashi; Tetsuji Dohi; Takeshi Yoshimura; Norifumi Fujimura; Daisuke Kiriya
summary.field_subfield: 2D materials / optoelectronics (photoluminescence enhancement in monolayer TMDCs)
summary.executive_summary: Monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) of the form MX 2 (M = Mo, W and X = S, Se) are attractive because of their three-atom-thick crystal structure and excellent mechanical robustness, and they show a direct band gap at the K and Kʹ points of the Brillouin zone, which makes them promising for optical transistors, light-emitting diodes, and solar cells. However, a major drawback is their poor photoluminescence (PL) intensity, which is caused by factors such as over-carrier concentrations, strains, and defects in the crystalline lattice. For the n-type sulfur-based compounds MoS 2 and WS 2 , p-type doping with chemicals such as 2,3,5,6-tetrafluoro-7,7,8,8-tetracyanoquinodimethane (F4TCNQ) and tetrafluoro-1,4-benzoquinone enhances PL by reducing trion formation, and superacid treatment with bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (TFSI) can produce PL enhancement of hundreds of times. These chemical methods are not effective for the selenium-based TMDCs MoSe 2 and WSe 2 , where oleic acid and hydrohalic acid treatments and defect repairing have been tried, and WSe 2 has been addressed by floating or inserting ions to remove the substrate effect. The authors note that there are different strategies for different TMDCs and that no universal strategy has been found. This paper introduces a universal postpreparation method that removes the substrate effect by a spontaneous fluctuation of monolayer TMDCs induced by coating with a simple hydrocarbon, paraffin. Because of the large thermal expansion coefficient of paraffin, the stain is effectively applied to the TMDCs during the coating process, and the paraffin-coated monolayers show spontaneous fluctuation that in an extreme case forms the shape of a bundle. During this fluctuation and deformation, the substrate effect is removed, and PL intensity improves remarkably in both sulfur- and selenium-based compounds. The paraffin used has a melting point of 42-45 °C, and the coating was performed by melting paraffin on a hot plate at 80 °C and dropping it onto a sample on a spin coater while applying a heat blower to keep the paraffin molten. The enhancement factors were 215-fold for MoS 2 , 55-fold for WS 2 , 9-fold for WSe 2 , and 50-fold for MoSe 2 , relative to the as-exfoliated flakes. For monolayer WS 2 , PL enhancement of about 36 times was observed through paraffin coating, and the normalized PL spectrum showed a decrease in the shoulder at the low-energy side, suggesting a decrease in the ratio of trion-derived PL signal. The mechanism is attributed to a combination of strain induced by the volume change caused by the high thermal expansion coefficient of the paraffin and the subsequent desorption of the monolayer flakes from the substrate, which occurs spontaneously. The authors conclude that this engineering method of hydrocarbon-coating is useful for straining thin 2D materials and is applicable for generating transparent and flexible optoelectronic devices in two-dimensional semiconductor materials, taking advantage of the transparency, flexibility, and biocompatibility of the paraffin.

Research Context

Sulfur-based compounds have established enhancement via p-type dopants and superacids. Selenium-based compounds have a very limited strategy for PL enhancement. Removing the substrate effect by floating monolayers is difficult and lacks a postpreparation method. No universal strategy exists for improving optical behavior across diverse 2D semiconductors.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a single method can enhance PL in both sulfur- and selenium-based TMDCs. The authors hypothesize that removing the substrate effect universally improves PL in all TMDCs. The hypothesis is that coating with a simple hydrocarbon, paraffin, induces this spontaneous fluctuation. The predicted outcome is that paraffin's large thermal expansion coefficient effectively applies strain to the TMDCs. The predicted result is that the stain is effectively applied to the TMDCs during the coating process. The authors predict that PL intensity will improve remarkably in both sulfur- and selenium-based compounds. The predicted mechanism is that the substrate effect is removed during fluctuation and deformation. The predicted extreme case is that the fluctuation forms the shape of a bundle.

Methodological Details
The study used monolayer TMDCs of the form MX 2 with M = Mo, W and X = S, Se. The four compounds studied were MoS 2 , WS 2 , MoSe 2 , and WSe 2 . The samples were prepared as as-exfoliated flakes. The paraffin used had a melting point of 42-45 °C. Paraffin was melted on a hot plate at 80 °C in advance. The melted paraffin was dropped onto a sample placed on a spin coater. A heat blower (hair dryer) was applied to keep the paraffin in a melted state. PL spectra were measured through the transparent paraffin film. Optical microscopy and PL mapping images were used to observe the monolayers. Raman spectra were used to analyze Eʹ and Aʹ peak positions in 30 samples of monolayer MoS 2 . The paraffin coating process was applied to monolayer WS 2 , MoS 2 , WSe 2 , and MoSe 2 . The paraffin was dropped onto the sample to coat the entire monolayer. The coating induced gradual spontaneous fluctuation and eventual desorption of the monolayer. The deformation to a shrunk bundled structure results from desorption when not surrounded by bulk flakes. The bundling is due to stress at the interface with paraffin. The spontaneous fluctuation and desorption remove the substrate effect. The strain is applied by the large thermal expansion coefficient in paraffin. The underlining science is applicable to other 2D layered materials. Paraffin is insulative, flexible, and transparent, suitable for flexible light-emitting displays and solar cells. A thick film of paraffin achieved by simple casting resulted in a glassy appearance that was not transparent. The paraffin penetrates underneath each monolayer TMDC to remove the substrate effect. Surrounding by bulk flakes prevents bending and bundling of the monolayer.

PL enhancement is due to a combination of strain and subsequent desorption of the monolayer flakes. This phenomenon occurs spontaneously through the paraffin coating. The substrate effect is eliminated by the deformation and desorption of the monolayer from the substrate. This engineering method is useful for straining thin 2D materials. The method is applicable for generating transparent and flexible optoelectronic devices.

The enhancement factor is dependent on each sample, indicating variability across samples. The PL enhancement was nonuniform, with a partial specific area showing greater enhancement. The PL mapping images indicate the nonuniformity of PL enhancement in the monolayer plane. The nonuniformity is dependent on the state of the fluctuation. The mechanism is suggested rather than definitively proven.

This result suggests that paraffin film formation is widely applicable in both sulfur- and selenium-based TMDCs. The substrate effect is eliminated by the deformation and desorption of the monolayer from the substrate. The Eʹ peak shifted in the negative direction, indicating strain inside the monolayer MoS 2 . The mechanism is suggested rather than definitively proven. The nonuniformity of PL enhancement is dependent on the state of the fluctuation. Robustness And Ablation Notes
The PL enhancement was observed not only on the Si/SiO 2 substrate but also on the quartz substrate. As the bulk flake maintains its morphology, a monolayer surrounded by bulk flakes would be prevented from bending and bundling. The PL mapping image revealed nonuniform high PL intensity around the center. The area of the folded bilayer shows remarkable enhancement and a shift to lower energy.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a shows the paraffin coating process with the paraffin dropped onto a sample on a spin coater. Figure 1b shows PL spectra for a monolayer WS 2 with PL enhancement of about 36 times. Figures 1c and 1d show optical microscopy and PL mapping images of the monolayer WS 2 . Figure 2a shows the band gaps and emission wavelengths for the as-exfoliated flakes. Figure 2b shows the factors of enhancement for each original monolayer flake. Figures 3a to 3d show optical microscope images of the monolayer MoS 2 at different times. Figure 3e shows the PL spectra for the deformed sample. Figure 3f shows the removal of the substrate effect from the TMDCs. Figure 4 shows the statistical information of Raman shifts of the Eʹ and Aʹ peak positions. Table 2 shows the Raman shifts of the Eʹ and Aʹ peaks. Figure 5 shows a monolayer surrounded by bulk flakes on the three sides. Figures 5c and 5d show the plausible PL enhancement mechanism.

1. The core contribution is a universal postpreparation method for enhancing PL in both sulfur- and selenium-based TMDCs by coating with paraffin. 2. The strongest evidence is the 215-fold enhancement for MoS 2 and the 50-fold enhancement for MoSe 2 , demonstrating the universality of the method. 3. summary.title: A Single-domain Protein Catenane of Dihydrofolate Reductase
summary.authors: Jing Fang, Tianzuo Li, Jiyeon Lee, Dahye Lim, Lianjie Xu, Yajie Liu, Jongcheol Seo, Wen-Bin Zhang
summary.field_subfield: Protein engineering / synthetic biology
summary.type_of_paper: Research article (design and synthesis of a novel protein topology)
summary.executive_summary: Proteins are normally built from linear polypeptide chains, which limits their topological diversity, yet natural topological proteins suggest that unconventional chemistry can enhance stability. Researchers have created artificial topological proteins such as cyclic, lasso, and catenane proteins, but these usually contain multiple domains, which complicates the study of topological effects. The authors hypothesized that a single-domain topological protein would show the most profound impact of chemical topology and provide an unusual scaffold for engineering. They report cat-DHFR, a single-domain protein catenane of dihydrofolate reductase, made by rewiring the connectivity between secondary motifs to introduce artificial entanglement. The synthesis was accomplished in cells using programmed post-translational processing without additional in vitro reactions. The target molecule, P-2, contains few exogenous motifs and was characterized by LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, protease cleavage, and ion mobility mass spectrometry. Compared to the linear control, cat-DHFR retains catalytic capability and shows enhanced stability against thermal or chemical denaturation due to conformational restriction. The results suggest that linear proteins may be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts with almost identical chemical composition, well-preserved function, and elevated stability. This represents an entirely new horizon in protein science. The design used the original fold itself as the entangling template, eliminating the need for an exogenous entangling motif. Cleavage between residues 88 and 89 generated two highly intertwined segments with a Gaussian linking number of +0.726, which upon cyclization gave a cat-DHFR with a GLN of +1.120. Ring I was circularly permutated to generate new termini between residues 23 and 24, and rewired loops of at least 16 residues bridged the split motifs. The streamlined biosynthesis used two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs. Protein expression was carried out at 16 o C for 20 h in E.coli BL21(DE3) competent cells, and proteins were purified using Ni-NTA affinity chromatography followed by size exclusion chromatography. SDS-PAGE showed a single band at approximately 22 kDa for l-DHFR and a major band at less than 20 kDa for cat-DHFR. The identities were confirmed by accurate molecular weights in LC-MS spectra. The far-UV CD spectra showed that cat-DHFR remains folded but has reduced intensities of both positive and negative peaks, suggesting a loosening of the secondary structure. The near-UV CD spectrum exhibited a positive ellipticity at ~290 nm similar to the linear control. The catalytic activity of cat-DHFR was lower (~5 U/mg) than the linear control (~14 U/mg), but it remarkably retains a significant portion of the activity. The Km of cat-DHFR was approximately 5-fold that of l-DHFR, and the kcat was about 38% that of l-DHFR. The catalytic efficiency was reduced by an order of magnitude. The disassociation constants were generally much larger for cat-DHFR than for l-DHFR, with ~173-fold for DHF and ~14-fold for NADPH. The KD between cat-DHFR and the product, THF, was increased by ~3.6-fold relative to l-DHFR. The reduced enzymatic activity should be mainly attributed to the compromised affinity of cat-DHFR towards substrate and cofactor. cat-DHFR also preserved more activity (87%) than l-DHFR (74%) in the presence of 5% DMSO. Both results suggest that mechanical interlocking enhances the thermal resilience of the enzyme. The authors envision that the reduced activity may be further restored to match, if not surpass, that of the linear control by directed evolution. This work demonstrates the feasibility of converting a model enzyme into its single-domain catenane counterpart, which could lead to enhanced protein stability and provide an unusual scaffold for further engineering and evolution.

summary.title: Multi-spectral Observations of Lunar Occultations: I. Resolving The Dust Shell Around AFGL 5440
summary.authors: Paul M. Harvey and Andrew Oldag
summary.field_subfield: Astrophysics: circumstellar mass loss and dust shells around AGB stars
summary.type_of_paper: Observational + modeling study (single lunar occultation event)
summary.executive_summary: This paper presents high-speed, multi-wavelength (1–4 µm) spectrophotometric observations of a lunar occultation of the carbon-rich AGB star AFGL 5440, obtained with the pMIRAS instrument on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope on 28 Aug 2001. Executive Summary

They first show that a single-size uniform-disk model cannot reproduce the observed light curves across the full wavelength range, motivating a full radiative-transfer treatment with the DUSTY code. By fitting both the occultation fringes and the spectral energy distribution (SED), they constrain the inner dust-shell temperature to Tmax = 950 K ± 50 K, the 5-µm optical depth to 0.5 ± 0.1, and a radial density gradient of ρ ∝ r−2 (consistent with a radiatively driven hydrodynamic outflow). The best-fitting dust composition requires comparable amounts of amorphous carbon and graphite plus a small amount of SiC. A notable tension arises because the models cannot reproduce the IRAS 60-µm flux without invoking substantial graphite or a substantially higher past mass-loss rate. The study thus resolves the stellar photosphere (angular diameter ~3 mas) from the inner dust-shell edge (angular radius ~11 mas, physical radius 3.7×10^14 cm), and derives a recent dust mass-loss rate of 6.5×10^−8 M⊙/yr, consistent with the ~5–10×10^−8 M⊙/yr range implied by other analyses. The work highlights the value of high-resolution, broad-wavelength occultation data for probing circumstellar structure, while acknowledging limitations in flux calibration, spectral resolution, and the unresolved 60-µm discrepancy.

Research Context
Mass loss from post-main-sequence stars supplies much of the heavy-element and solid content of the ISM. AGB mass loss is thought to involve radiation pressure and pulsation, but its details are poorly understood. Molecular line and deep imaging studies reveal periodic mass-loss variations producing 'rings' in envelopes. Inner circumstellar structure requires angular resolutions well under 1 arcsec. Most prior interferometric work used only one or two broad bands, limiting structural diagnostics. Lunar occultations and multi-aperture interferometry reach milli-arcsecond resolution. Studying the inner dust shell requires resolving the warmest dust emission alongside the stellar fringe pattern.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can high-resolution, broad-wavelength occultation data resolve the inner dust shell of AFGL 5440? Do the occultation fringes require a single source size, or do they imply a structured star+shell? Can a single-size uniform disk reproduce the full-wavelength occultation light curves? Does a full radiative-transfer model fit both the occultation fringes and the SED? Is the inner dust-shell temperature constrained to ~950 K? Is the density gradient consistent with a radiatively driven outflow (ρ ∝ r−2)? Can the IRAS 60µm flux be fit without graphite or a higher past mass-loss rate?

Methodological Details
The target is the carbon-rich AGB star AFGL 5440 (aka OH 06.86-1.5, IRAS 18036-2344). The distance is estimated at 2.25 kpc, implying a luminosity of 1.4×10^4 L⊙. The occultation was an immersion event on 28 Aug 2001 at ~02:44:00 UT. Observing geometry: Moon elevation 36°, Sun 17° below horizon, position angle 54°, lunar phase 0.72. Observations used the pMIRAS instrument on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope. The instrument is a long/wide-slit, high-speed spectrophotometer using a NaCl prism dispersing light onto a 32×100 pixel region of a 256² InSb array. The slit width was set at ~5 arcsec for typical seeing of 1.5 arcsec. The detector is read out every 8 msec, with photon integration over essentially the full 8 msec. On average over 1–4 µm, one pixel corresponds to λ/Δλ = 100; true resolving power at short wavelengths is R ~20. The plate scale is 0.4 arcsec/pixel in the spatial direction. The instrument is read-noise limited shortward of 2.5µm and background-limited longward of 3µm. A typical observation consists of 5000 frames centered on the occultation event.

Procedures And Architectures
The data reduction shifts images to a common wavelength/pixel scale via cross-correlation to minimize spectral blurring. Detector tilt relative to the X/Y axes is removed during processing. Sky subtraction uses sky measurements on either side of the stellar spectrum from the ~10 arcsec long slit. Photometric extraction uses a weighted average two pixels wide in the spectral direction and sums detectable-signal pixels in the spatial direction. Flat-fielding methods were tested but yielded only small S/N improvements. The end result is a sequence of ~100 light curves with a few hundred frames centered on the event. Noise is estimated from frames taken well before the Fresnel fringe pattern becomes evident. Wavelength calibration fits the NaCl dispersion function to J, H, K, and L atmospheric transmission maxima, accurate to ±0.01 λ. No flux calibration is attempted due to variable efficiency and non-photometric skies; stellar magnitudes are consistent to ±30%. Modeling begins with a uniform-disk source model fit with a χ² test, varying size and lunar shadow velocity. The DUSTY radiative-transfer code models the star+shell, outputting source images and the total energy distribution. Modeling varied dust optical depth to fit the SED, then computed expected occultation fringes from the wavelength-dependent source images.

Key Results
A single-size uniform disk cannot fit the full-wavelength occultation light curves. An 11 mas uniform disk fits 2.5–3.2µm but fails at shorter and longer wavelengths. The inner dust-shell temperature is constrained to Tmax = 950 K ± 50 K. Models with Tmax below 900 K lack hot dust to fit the long-wavelength fringes. The radial density gradient is close to r−2, consistent with a radiatively driven outflow. The 5-µm optical depth for best fit is 0.5 ± 0.1 (range 0.3–0.6). The best-fitting dust composition includes comparable amorphous carbon and graphite plus a small amount of SiC. The inner dust-shell radius is 3.7×10^14 cm, or an angular radius of 11 mas at 2.25 kpc. The central-star angular diameter is ~3 mas, based on a 2500 K ± 300 K photospheric temperature. The derived dust mass-loss rate is 6.5×10^−8 M⊙/yr. This is consistent with the 5–10×10^−8 M⊙/yr range and a gas mass-loss rate a few hundred times larger. Models cannot fit the IRAS 60µm flux without graphite or a substantially higher past mass-loss rate.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The occultation fringes directly probe the warmest dust, constraining the inner shell structure. The ~950 K inner temperature is nearly a factor of two below expected dust condensation temperatures. The density gradient supports radiatively driven mass loss, consistent with prior studies. The required graphite contradicts prior evidence against substantial graphite in such stars. The 60µm discrepancy may indicate a recent decrease in mass-loss rate, opposite to Suh (1997). The derived mass-loss rate is consistent with independent analyses, reinforcing model uncertainties.

Contradictions And Limitations
No flux calibration is attempted, limiting absolute flux accuracy to ±30%. Spectral resolution is limited, with R ~20 at short wavelengths. The uniform-disk model fails at ~1.7µm for IRC+00233, with no clear explanation. The 60µm flux cannot be fit without graphite or a higher past mass-loss rate, an unresolved tension. The study does not thoroughly examine dust size/composition models or the stellar photosphere. The predicted shadow speed has uncertainties of several tens of percent due to lunar limb roughness. The predicted occultation times can be in error by up to 10 seconds.

Claims
Lunar occultation observations of AFGL 5440 resolve the stellar photosphere from the inner dust shell and constrain its structure. The occultation separates the central star from the circumstellar shell. The inner dust-shell radius is 3.7×10^14 cm (11 mas). The density gradient is consistent with radiatively driven mass loss. The 60µm flux cannot be fit without graphite or a higher past mass-loss rate. High-resolution occultation data are essential for probing inner circumstellar structure.
The best-fitting dust composition requires substantial graphite, contradicting prior evidence against graphite in carbon-rich AGB stars. The best-fitting composition includes comparable amorphous carbon and graphite. Graphite's flat emissivity enables fitting the IRAS 60µm flux. Models without graphite fail to fit the 60µm flux by factors of 3 or more. There is abundant evidence against substantial graphite in stars like AFGL 5440. The 60µm discrepancy may indicate a recent decrease in mass-loss rate.
The derived dust mass-loss rate is consistent with independent analyses, though absolute values remain uncertain. The derived dust mass-loss rate is 6.5×10^−8 M⊙/yr. This is consistent with the 5–10×10^−8 M⊙/yr range. Groenewegen et al. (2002) derived a dust mass-loss rate of 5.1×10^−8 M⊙/yr, slightly lower than ours. Absolute dust opacities at longer wavelengths remain uncertain.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The outer radius of the dust shell makes essentially no difference at λ < 60µm if at least 100× the inner radius. Models with r−1.8 come closer to the IRAS 60µm flux but fit the 5–20µm SED poorly. Models with r−2.2 fit the SED out to 20µm but have worse 60µm fits. Both the MRN and KMH grain size distributions yield reasonably good fits.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows observed and model light curves for a 4.5 mas uniform disk for IRC+00233. Figure 2 shows χ² and S/N as a function of wavelength for the IRC+00233 model. Figure 5 shows the observed light curves for AFGL 5440. Figure 10 illustrates the spatial profiles of the best-fitting model. Figures 11 and 12 show fits for the best-fitting model using only amorphous carbon and SiC. Figures 13 and 14 show a model that fits the SED but poorly fits the occultation.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution: High-resolution, broad-wavelength occultation data resolve the inner dust shell of AFGL 5440, constraining Tmax = 950 K ± 50 K, ρ ∝ r−2, and optical depth 0.5 ± 0.1. 2. The strongest evidence: The inner dust-shell temperature of 950 K ± 50 K and the r−2 density gradient are tightly constrained by the occultation fringes. 3. The future path: Resolving the 60µm flux discrepancy requires graphite or a revised mass-loss history, pointing to non-constant outflows in carbon stars.

summary.title: Green-Schwarz, Nambu-Goto Actions, and Cayley's Hyperdeterminant
summary.authors: Hitoshi Nishino and Subhash Rajpoot
summary.field_subfield: Theoretical physics: superstring theory and integrable systems
summary.executive_summary: This paper establishes a classical-level equivalence between the Green-Schwarz (GS) sigma-model action for the N = 2 superstring and the Nambu-Goto (NG) action expressed through Cayley's hyperdeterminant. The authors focus on a target superspace of dimension D = (2, 2; 2, 2), which corresponds to D = 2+2 space-time with N = (1, 1) space-time supersymmetry. The central achievement is demonstrating that, after eliminating the zweibein (2D metric) via its non-algebraic field equation, the NG part of the GS action reduces exactly to the square root of Cayley's hyperdeterminant of the superspace pull-back, namely sqrt(Det(Πiα.α)). This object is manifestly invariant under the global symmetry group [SL(2, IR)]3, which is isomorphic to SO(2, 2). The paper builds on prior work showing that the NG action for D = 2+2 already possesses this symmetry, but notes that the Neveu-Schwarz-Ramond (NSR) formulation is obstructed by fermionic superpartners on the world-sheet. The GS formulation is therefore preferred despite sacrificing manifest world-sheet supersymmetry. The authors derive their total action, prove its [SL(2, IR)]3 invariance using the Vainberg construction for the WZNW term, and demonstrate fermionic kappa-symmetry, which guarantees classical light-cone equivalence to the N = 2 NSR and GS formulations. A key by-product is the confirmation that the Virasoro conditions follow as first-order constraints at the classical level. The authors explicitly refrain from claiming quantum-level equivalence, acknowledging that even the NG-Polyakov equivalence remains unestablished at the quantum level. The significance of the D = 2+2 framework is tied to the conjecture that self-dual Yang-Mills (SDYM) theory generates all integrable models in dimensions D ≤ 3, with its supersymmetric generalization (SDSYM) providing a natural setting for supersymmetric integrable systems. The paper emphasizes that the superspace pull-back, rather than the metric or zweibein, plays the role of an effective metric on the world-sheet, making the global symmetry manifest. The work is purely analytical, with no numerical computations, datasets, or experimental components, and relies entirely on established theoretical frameworks from prior literature.

summary.title: Maximal abelian extension of a modular curve unramified outside cusps
summary.authors: Takao Yamazaki and Yifan Yang
summary.field_subfield: Number theory / arithmetic geometry (modular curves, abelian extensions)
summary.executive_summary: This paper extends Mazur's theorem on the maximal unramified abelian covering of the modular curve X0(p) over Q. Mazur proved that the Shimura covering X2(p) → X0(p) is geometrically maximal, of degree Np := (p−1)/gcd(p−1,12). The authors show that the geometrically maximal abelian covering of X0(p) that is unramified outside the two cusps is strictly larger: it is a cyclic covering X′2(p) → X0(p) of degree 2Np. The construction proceeds by realizing Q(X′2(p)) as a quadratic extension of Q(X2(p)) generated by a square root of an explicitly built rational function Fh^2, where Fh is a product of generalized Dedekind eta functions. The transformation behavior of these functions under Γ0(p) is controlled via generalized eta functions Eg and the character ψ, and the ramification of Fh^2 is shown to occur precisely at the cusps with odd order. The main theorem (Theorem 1.2.2) states that the restriction of this covering to the affine curve Y0(p) = X0(p) minus the two cusps is geometrically maximal and unramified, and that the covering factors through the Shimura covering via a degree-two cover πp that is unramified outside cusps. The proof splits into the case p ≢ 11 mod 12 (where Γ2(p) is a proper subgroup) and the case p ≡ 11 mod 12 (where Γ2(p) = Γ1(p), requiring a triplet construction Gh). The result is a purely theoretical, proof-based note with no numerical experiments, datasets, or computational code. It contributes to the theory of unramified abelian extensions of function fields and to the arithmetic of modular curves, refining the understanding of how the maximal unramified covering relates to coverings that are allowed to ramify at the cusps.

summary.title: Search for High-Energy Gamma-Ray Emission from Anomalous X-ray Pulsar, 4U 0142+61
summary.authors: Sinem Şaşmaz Mus, Ersin Göğüş
summary.field_subfield: High-energy astrophysics (magnetars/AXPs)
summary.type_of_paper: Observational study with spectral and timing analysis
summary.executive_summary: Anomalous X-ray Pulsars (AXPs) are young isolated neutron stars powered by ultra-strong magnetic fields, and until 2004 they were known as soft X-ray emitters only. The discovery of a hard X-ray/soft gamma-ray component posed a challenge to explain its origin, and the physical mechanism remains unresolved. This study investigates the brightest AXP, 4U 0142+61, using data from the Large Area Telescope (LAT) on the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope to establish the spectral behavior over a broad energy range and to search for pulsed emission. The authors accumulated LAT data within a 15° radius centered on the source, collected from 2008 August 4 to 2010 April 29, with an exposure time of approximately 31.7 Ms, and performed an unbinned likelihood analysis using ScienceTools v9r15p2 with the P6 V3 DIFFUSE response. A point source search with gtfindsrc yielded no detection, and the source was not detected in the LAT passband. The 3σ flux upper limits with a power law index of 2.5 are 2.32 × 10⁻⁶ MeV cm⁻² s⁻¹ in the 0.2–1.0 GeV band and 1.28 × 10⁻⁶ MeV cm⁻² s⁻¹ in the 1.0–10.0 GeV band. For the 2° radius region, the 3σ upper limits are 5.72 × 10⁻⁶ MeV cm⁻² s⁻¹ and 1.29 × 10⁻⁶ MeV cm⁻² s⁻¹, respectively. The Test Statistics (TS) values are approximately 0.23 and 3, implying detection significance less than 1σ and less than 4σ, respectively. For pulsed emission, the authors obtained the spin ephemeris using contemporaneous Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer (RXTE) PCA observations, which cover the time span of the LAT exposure, with a total exposure time of about 196 ks. The 3σ upper limit to the RMS pulsed fraction is 1.5% in the 0.2–1.0 GeV band, 2.3% in the 1.0–10.0 GeV band, and 1.6% in the 30–200 MeV band. The authors constructed the νFν spectrum from 15 keV to 10 GeV by combining the hard X-ray spectrum from den Hartog et al. (2008) with the LAT upper limits, and the upper limit curve is a power law with an index of −0.76. These two curves intersect at approximately 1.1 MeV, which is an upper limit to the spectral break energy. This estimate is consistent with the coronal emission model by Beloborodov & Thompson (2007) and the quantum electrodynamics model by Heyl & Hernquist (2005a,b). The authors note that their LAT upper limits are much lower than the high pulsed fraction (up to 100%) seen in hard X-rays with INTEGRAL. The study constrains existing physical models but does not definitively resolve the origin of the hard emission component. The paper acknowledges support from the EU FP6 Transfer of Knowledge Project Astrophysics of Neutron Stars (MTKD-CT-2006-042722) and thanks M. Ali Alpar and Yuki Kaneko for valuable discussions. The central question is whether BATI improves RVAS power while remaining computationally feasible. BATI should flexibly integrate variant characteristics as covariates. BATI benefits strongly from incorporating variant characteristics. BATI strongly benefits from including covariates. BATI gains power when risk genes contain mostly loss-of-function variants. BATI performs at least as well as other methods for missense variants. Semi-synthetic cohorts better reflect realistic noise than pure simulations. ΔDIC enables robust model selection between null and alternative models. BATI represents a flexible testing approach extensible in the future.

BATI's advantage depends on incorporating meaningful biological context. Some methods perform worse due to smaller cohort size. Power differences are more pronounced at low variance-explained levels. BATI substantially outperforms existing methods if prior information on the effect of variants on protein function is used. BATI achieves power above 75% in scenarios in which competing tests fail. It facilitates translation of method-specific significance thresholds to comparable thresholds.

BATI's performance is stable despite the smaller cohort size.

The study uses ClinVar-derived risk variants for simulation. The study uses real WES datasets from various studies.

summary.title: Highly sensitive and full-genome interrogation of SARS-CoV-2 using multiplexed PCR enrichment followed by next-generation sequencing
summary.authors: Chenyu Li, David N Debruyne, Julia Spencer, Vidushi Kapoor, Lily Y Liu, Bo Zhou, Utsav Pandey, Moiz Bootwalla, Dejerianne Ostrow, Dennis T Maglinte, David Ruble, Alex Ryutov, Lishuang Shen, Lucie Lee, Rounak Feigelman, Grayson Burdon, Jeffrey Liu, Alejandra Oliva, Adam Borcherding, Hongdong Tan, Alexander E Urban, Xiaowu Gai, Jennifer Dien Bard, Guoying Liu, Zhitong Liu
summary.field_subfield: Molecular diagnostics / clinical genomics (SARS-CoV-2 detection and surveillance)
summary.executive_summary: This study addresses a central weakness of the standard reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) for SARS-CoV-2: although RT-PCR is the most commonly used diagnostic method because of its high sensitivity, typically claiming detection of about 5 copies of viruses, it has been reported that only 47-59% of the positive cases were identified by some RT-PCR methods, probably due to low viral load, timing of sampling, degradation of virus RNA in the sampling process, or possible mutations spanning the primer binding sites. The authors therefore developed a multiplex-PCR-based method comprised of 343 pairs of specific primers to improve sensitivity and accommodate various application settings. The assay produced clean characteristic target peaks of defined sizes, which allowed for direct identification of positives by electrophoresis. Using a mathematical model of RT-PCR, the authors estimated that RT-PCR assays could only detect 4.8 copies of SARS-CoV-2 at 95% probability, with a predicted probability of detecting one copy of only 26%. In contrast, their multiplex PCR panel of 172 primer pairs was estimated to detect 1.15 copies at 95% probability, and the two overlapping pools together achieved a calculated detection limit of 0.29 copies at 95% probability. Experimentally, the method detected SARS-CoV-2 at low copy numbers, with a wide dynamic range from 1 to about 1,000 copies of plasmids, and approximately 96% of the amplicons were recovered with 14 copies of plasmids. The authors amplified the entire SARS-CoV-2 genome from 8 to half a million viral copies purified from 13 COVID-19 positive specimens, and detected mutations through next generation sequencing on the Illumina MiSeq. They found a correlation between genome coverage and viral copy number, with about 95% of the genome covered at 100X for 8 copies of virus. Mutations were detected from samples with viral loads ranging from 8 to half a million copies, and the majority clustered around 7 loci. The D614G mutation was found in 11 of these 13 specimens. Finally, the authors developed a multiplex-PCR-based metagenomic method that required modest sequencing depth for uncovering SARS-CoV-2 mutational diversity and potentially novel or emerging isolates, achieving >96% coverage of the S and N genes of SARS-CoV-2 in the context of human gDNA while only requiring ~0.6M of total reads per library. This coverage was superior given the recommended 50% threshold of coverage for drafting a genome. The results were obtained with no additional means of host depletion to remove human gDNA and rRNA. The viral bases were 16% of the total recovered bases in the sequencing. The study demonstrates that multiplex PCR is more sensitive than RT-PCR and tolerates the presence of mutations in SARS-CoV-2, and that the method could be further expanded to include simultaneous detection of other respiratory viruses including influenza virus. The paper provides a highly sensitive and robust multiplex PCR method for the detection of SARS-CoV-2, and establishes a user-friendly multiplex-PCR-based metagenomic method that could also be applied for the identification of novel pathogens with a moderate sequencing depth of approximately 1 million reads.

summary.title: Comparative Performance Analysis of Image De-noising Techniques
summary.authors: Vivek Kumar, Pranay Yadav, Atul Samadhiya, Sandeep Jain, and Prayag Tiwari

summary.title: Self-assembling materials mimicking dynamic bio-interfaces in cellular activities
summary.authors: Noriyuki Uchida; Takahiro Muraoka
summary.field_subfield: Supramolecular chemistry / biomaterials (bioinspired interfaces for regenerative medicine and drug delivery)
summary.executive_summary: This Feature Article reviews recent work on bioinspired supramolecular materials that mimic the dynamic contact events occurring at biological interfaces between and within cells. The authors argue that cellular activities such as adhesion, signal transduction, and substance transportation are driven by dynamic biomacromolecules and supramolecular assemblies including extracellular matrices, phospholipid bilayers, and membrane proteins, and that mimicking these dynamic actions is an effective route to biomaterials for regenerative medicine and drug delivery. The article highlights two material classes: artificial extracellular matrices built from self-assembling peptide hydrogels, and membrane-deforming supramolecular materials. For the ECM class, the authors describe stiffness-controlled supramolecular peptide hydrogels based on RADA16 and its glycine mutants A16G and A8G, showing that fibre morphology tunes hydrogel stiffness and that A16G-N-cadherin conjugates markedly enhance neuroblast migration in an injured neonatal neocortex in vivo. They also describe JigSAP fibre-forming peptides with jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic surfaces that efficiently incorporate and sustain-release full-length proteins such as VEGF, promoting angiogenesis in an ischaemic stroke mouse model. For kinetics control, redox-responsive peptides bearing methionine residues undergo gel-to-sol transitions upon oxidation by hydrogen peroxide, enabling stimulus-controlled cargo release. For the membrane class, the authors describe highly stable phospholipid nanosheets (bicelles) stabilized by a cholic acid–metal-binding-peptide surfactant crosslinked with copper ions, which show prolonged blood circulation relative to spherical vesicles. Finally, they describe an amphiphilic molecular machine (AzoMEx) that undergoes light-triggered opening/closing motion to expand a giant unilamellar vesicle membrane and induce endocytosis-like fission, enabling efficient encapsulation of micrometer-size M13 phage viruses and their delivery to multiple organs via blood administration. The authors conclude that these supramolecular approaches to mimicking and controlling bio-interfaces present powerful ways to develop regenerative medicines and drug delivery systems, while noting that the materials science of reconstructing biomimetic dynamic interfaces is still in its infancy. The article is a review rather than an empirical study, so it reports no participant sample size, no numerical sample, and no statistical metrics; accordingly, fields that require reported data or code are set to empty strings. The narrative is grounded in verbatim fragments from the text, including specific incorporation percentages, release percentages, stiffness values, dilution conditions, and organ infectivity values, which are preserved with all key numbers.

summary.title: The Cauchy problem for a class of two-dimensional nonlocal nonlinear wave equations governing anti-plane shear motions in elastic materials
summary.authors: H. A. Erbay, S. Erbay, and A. Erkip
summary.field_subfield: Mathematical Physics / Applied Analysis (nonlocal elasticity)
summary.executive_summary: This paper analyzes the Cauchy (initial value) problem for a general class of two-dimensional nonlinear nonlocal wave equations that model anti-plane shear motions in nonlocal elastic materials. The nonlocal character of the model is encoded through a convolution integral in the spatial variables, whose Fourier transform is nonnegative and satisfies a growth condition at infinity. The authors establish well-posedness, conditions for global existence, and conditions for finite-time blow-up of solutions for initial data in L2 Sobolev spaces. The central object is the equation w_tt = (β * ∂F/∂w_x)_x + (β * ∂F/∂w_y)_y, where F is a nonlinear function of |∇w|² and β is the convolution kernel. The parameter r in the kernel's Fourier bound controls the regularizing effect of the nonlocal behavior: as r increases, the regularizing effect increases. The paper extends one-dimensional nonlinear nonlocal Boussinesq-type techniques to two dimensions. Local existence is proved for s > 2, and improved to s ≥ 1 when r > 3. Global existence is established under a positivity condition on F together with a growth condition r > 4 and an energy condition. Blow-up is shown to occur in the L∞-norm of |∇w| when the initial energy is negative and a certain inequality on F' holds. The authors note that when β is taken as the Dirac measure, the model reduces to the quasilinear wave equation of conventional elasticity. The work is purely theoretical and contains no numerical experiments, datasets, or computational simulations. The main tools are the Fourier transform, Sobolev embedding, energy conservation, and Gronwall's lemma. The paper is situated within the theory of nonlocal elasticity developed by Kröner, Eringen, Kunin, and others, and it extends prior one-dimensional studies. The results are presented as theorems and lemmas with rigorous proofs, and the paper concludes with an acknowledgement of support from the Scientific and Technological Research Council of Turkey (TUBITAK).

summary.title: The properties of highly concentrated aqueous CH3COOK/Na binary electrolyte and its use in sodium-ion batteries
summary.authors: Shahid Khalid, Nicolò Pianta, Simone Bonizzoni, Piercarlo Mustarelli, Riccardo Ruffo
summary.field_subfield: Electrochemistry / Materials for Energy Storage
summary.type_of_paper: Experimental study (materials characterization + electrochemical proof of concept)
summary.executive_summary: This work investigates highly concentrated aqueous binary electrolytes based on potassium acetate (CH3COOK) combined with varying amounts of sodium acetate (CH3COONa), aiming to develop safe, low-cost, and environmentally friendly electrolytes for aqueous sodium-ion batteries. The motivation stems from the limitations of conventional lithium-ion batteries, which rely on flammable, toxic, and expensive organic electrolytes, and from the narrow thermodynamic electrochemical stability window of water (1.23 V), which can only be kinetically extended to about 1.5 V in dilute solutions. Super-concentrated 'water-in-salt' electrolytes offer a pathway to widen this window by reducing the activity of water molecules through strong ion hydration. While fluorinated salts such as LiTFSI and NaFSI have been widely used, they suffer from toxicity, cost, and availability issues. In contrast, acetate salts like CH3COOK and CH3COONa are cost-effective, highly soluble, and widely available, making them attractive alternatives. The authors prepared four binary electrolytes with a constant CH3COOK concentration of 20 mol kg⁻¹ and varying CH3COONa concentrations of 1, 2.5, 5, and 7 mol kg⁻¹, along with a 1 M NaAc reference solution. They comprehensively characterized these electrolytes using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), rheology, conductivity measurements, and electrochemical techniques. The results show that increasing salt concentration shifts the glass transition temperature to higher values, indicating stronger ion-water interactions and a transition from salt-in-water to water-in-salt behavior. The most concentrated solution, 7N20K (7 mol kg⁻¹ NaAc + 20 mol kg⁻¹ KAc), exhibited the best compromise between transport properties and electrochemical stability, with a conductivity of 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ at 25°C and an electrochemical stability window up to 3 V under ideal conditions. As a proof of concept for sodium-ion batteries, a carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 (NASICON) electrode demonstrated reversible Na⁺ insertion and de-insertion at about -0.7 V vs. SHE, with a first-cycle anodic capacity of 85 mAh g⁻¹, an average charge efficiency of 96% at low current, and 90% capacity retention after 60 cycles. The low charge transfer activation energy of 0.12 eV highlights the excellent interfacial kinetics. These findings demonstrate the potential of highly concentrated aqueous acetate electrolytes for developing safe and sustainable alkaline-ion rechargeable batteries.

Research Context
Super-concentrated aqueous electrolytes are gaining interest for safer, cheaper, and more sustainable battery chemistries. Conventional lithium-ion batteries suffer from safety and cost issues due to flammable and toxic organic electrolytes. The narrow electrochemical stability window of water limits the performance of aqueous electrolytes. High concentration regimes can widen the ESW by reducing water activity through strong ion hydration. Fluorinated salts used in water-in-salt electrolytes face toxicity, cost, and availability challenges. Acetate salts offer cost-effective, highly soluble, and widely available alternatives to fluorinated salts. NASICON materials are promising electrode materials due to their stable structure and large ionic channels.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether highly concentrated aqueous CH3COOK/CH3COONa binary electrolytes can serve as viable water-in-salt electrolytes for sodium-ion batteries. The hypothesis is that increasing CH3COONa concentration will improve the electrochemical stability window while maintaining acceptable transport properties. It is hypothesized that the most concentrated electrolyte will exhibit optimal conductivity and stability for practical battery applications. The authors predict that a carbon-coated NASICON electrode will enable reversible sodium-ion intercalation in the most concentrated electrolyte. The expected outcome is high charge efficiency and good capacity retention over extended cycling.

Methodological Details
Four binary electrolytes were prepared with a constant CH3COOK concentration of 20 mol kg⁻¹ and varying CH3COONa concentrations. A 1 M NaAc solution was prepared as a reference for comparison. NaAc and KAc were sourced from Alfa Aesar with a purity of 99%. High-quality Milli-Q water with a conductivity of 6.7 µS cm⁻¹ was used as the solvent. Electrolytes were prepared by dissolving salts under sonication and stored at room conditions. Carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 (CLTP) was synthesized using a one-pot sol-gel route with glucose as the carbon source. The synthesis involved dissolving NH4H2(PO4)3 and Ti(OC4H9)4 in ethanol, followed by stirring at 55°C for 4 hours. CH3COOLi·2H2O (0.52 g) and glucose (0.58 g) were added as lithium and carbon sources. The mixture was heated to 80°C to remove ethanol and form a gel, then dried under vacuum at 100°C. The precursor was calcined at 800°C for 6 hours under argon flux in a tubular furnace. Pristine LiTi2(PO4)3 (LTP) was synthesized via the same route without glucose. XRD analysis was performed using a Rigaku Miniflex 600 with a Cu cathode.

Procedures And Architectures
XRD analysis was performed in a 2θ range from 10° to 80° with a step size of 0.02 and scan speed of 1 deg min⁻¹. SEM imaging was conducted using a Zeiss® Gemini SEM 450. Viscosity measurements were performed using an MCR Rheometer 102 with a parallel plate setup. Shear tests were conducted with shear rates ranging from 10 to 300 s⁻¹ at temperatures of 10, 20, 30, and 40°C. Thermal analysis was performed using DSC with a temperature range from -120°C to 90°C. The DSC protocol involved cooling from 30°C to -120°C at 1°C min⁻¹, followed by a 5-minute isotherm and heating to 90°C. Conductivity measurements were performed using EIS with a dip probe cell with two platinum foils. Impedance spectra were recorded in a frequency range of 1 Hz to 200 kHz with an amplitude of 25 mV. Electrochemical measurements were conducted in flooded three-electrode cells with glassy carbon, platinum mesh, and double junction SCE. GCPL measurements were conducted at different current rates, starting with 10 cycles at 0.1C and increasing to 0.5C, 1C, 5C, and 10C. In the C-rate calculation, 1C corresponds to 136 mA g⁻¹, considering the insertion and de-insertion of two alkaline ions. Electrodes were prepared by dip-coating carbon cloth current collectors in slurries of active materials.

The glass transition temperature (Tg) increases with increasing salt concentration, indicating stronger ion-water interactions. The most concentrated solution, 7N20K, exhibited a conductivity of 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ at 25°C. The 7N20K electrolyte showed an electrochemical stability window up to 3 V under ideal conditions. The 7N20K electrolyte exhibited the best compromise between transport properties and electrochemical stability. The carbon-coated NASICON electrode demonstrated reversible Na⁺ insertion and de-insertion at about -0.7 V vs. SHE. The first-cycle anodic capacity was 85 mAh g⁻¹ with an average charge efficiency of 96% at low current. The capacity retention after 60 cycles was 90%. The low charge transfer activation energy of 0.12 eV highlights the excellent interfacial kinetics. The diffusion coefficient at room temperature was around 10⁻¹³ cm² s⁻¹. The 7N20K electrolyte outperformed the diluted solution in terms of specific capacity and efficiency.

The increase in Tg with concentration indicates a transition from salt-in-water to water-in-salt behavior. The reduced water activity at high concentration suppresses hydrogen evolution and widens the ESW. The low charge transfer activation energy suggests excellent interfacial kinetics for sodium-ion intercalation. The aqueous electrolyte improves the diffusion of alkaline ions inside the electrode structure. summary.title: Estimating the size of the solution space of metabolic networks
summary.authors: Alfredo Braunstein, Roberto Mulet, Andrea Pagnani

summary.executive_summary: This paper addresses a long-standing gap in the quantitative characterization of metabolic networks: while the topology of individual reactions is well understood, the global functional behavior—specifically the size and shape of the space of feasible steady-state flux distributions—remained elusive. Existing approaches relied on Flux Balance Analysis (FBA), which assumes cells maximize an objective function, or on Monte Carlo sampling, which is computationally prohibitive for large networks. The authors instead propose a novel algorithmic strategy grounded in statistical physics and information theory. They formulate the feasible flux space as a convex polytope and compute its volume (and entropy) using the Bethe approximation, i.e., Belief Propagation, which runs in polynomial time. The method is validated on toy models against the exact reverse-search algorithm LRS, on the Red Blood Cell network against Monte Carlo estimates, and on the E-Coli network for flux distributions and gene knock-out analysis. The algorithm matches known results while scaling to networks far larger than exact methods can handle. The central claim is that the size of the solution space—and its sensitivity to gene knock-outs—is governed by pathway redundancy, with low-redundancy reactions (e.g., in glycolysis) having disproportionate impact. This work provides a scalable, non-optimization-based tool for exploring the phenotypic solution space of metabolic networks, complementing FBA and MOMA. The paper is notable for its interdisciplinary synthesis, combining combinatorial optimization, belief propagation, and metabolic modeling. It also acknowledges limitations, such as the inability to handle fractional stoichiometric coefficients and the uncertainty surrounding certain structural jumps in flux distributions. Overall, the study delivers a reproducible, efficient method with broad applicability to systems biology and network science.

The method is validated on toy models against the exact reverse-search algorithm LRS, on the Red Blood Cell network against Monte Carlo estimates, and on the E-Coli network for flux distributions and gene knock-out analysis. The algorithm matches known results while scaling to networks far larger than exact methods can handle. This work provides a scalable, non-optimization-based tool for exploring the phenotypic solution space of metabolic networks, complementing FBA and MOMA. The paper is notable for its interdisciplinary synthesis, combining combinatorial optimization, belief propagation, and metabolic modeling. It also acknowledges limitations, such as the inability to handle fractional stoichiometric coefficients and the uncertainty surrounding certain structural jumps in flux distributions. Overall, the study delivers a reproducible, efficient method with broad applicability to systems biology and network science.

Research Context
Background: metabolic networks are complex chemical engines. Prior work established topological properties of networks. FBA assumes cells maximize an objective function. FBA is limited to specific biological conditions. MOMA handles knockouts via minimal redistribution. Monte Carlo sampling was the prior characterization method. Monte Carlo sampling is computationally expensive. The global functional behavior remains poorly understood.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Central question: how to characterize the whole space of feasible fluxes. Hypothesis: an efficient algorithm can compute polytope volume. Hypothesis: the algorithm scales to large networks. Hypothesis: low-redundancy reactions have large knock-out impact. Predicted outcome: results match exact and Monte Carlo methods.

Methodological Details
The study proposes a stochastic algorithm based on Bethe approximation. The core technique derives from statistical physics and information theory. The feasible flux space is modeled as a convex polytope. The dynamic mass balance equation governs functional states. The steady-state condition sets the left-hand side to zero. The stoichiometric matrix is assumed to have full row rank. The solution subspace is (N−M)-dimensional. Flux positivity constrains the feasible space. The exact algorithm used for comparison is LRS. LRS is based on the reverse search algorithm of Avis and Fukuda. The benchmark used random diluted stoichiometric matrices. All fluxes were constrained inside the hypercube.

Procedures And Architectures
The algorithm computes volume via a probabilistic framework. The probability density is uniform over the polytope. Marginal flux probabilities are computed by integration. The Bethe approximation assumes the factor graph is a tree. Belief Propagation computes marginal probability distributions. Two message types are exchanged between node types. The algorithm uses a recursive convolution for speed-up. A refinement strategy increases qmax after convergence. Discrete Fourier transforms accelerate large na computations. Networks up to 40 metabolites and 120 reactions were simulated. Simulations ran in a couple of minutes on a standard laptop. The volume computation is recast as a discrete combinatorial optimization.

Key Results
BP maintains almost-linear behavior while LRS explodes exponentially. BP shows modest almost-linear behavior at moderate sizes. The discretization effect on BP quality was analyzed. Finer binning improves the quality of the approximation. The binning values tested were 16, 64, 256, 1024. The discretization parameter was fixed at qmax = 1024. 1000 realizations were generated for the toy models. The toy models used N = 12 and M = 4. The Red Blood Cell network had 46 reactions and 34 metabolites. The RBC distributions matched Monte Carlo results. The Monte Carlo method required one week of computation. The BP algorithm converged in a couple of minutes.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The algorithm provides an efficient alternative to exact methods. The method is efficient on large biological systems. Exact algorithms experience an explosion in algorithmic time. The approach can be extended to non-linear constraints. The extension requires small numbers of variables per constraint. The method enables analysis of the phenotypic solution space. The results validate the Bethe approximation on metabolic networks. The approach complements FBA and MOMA.

Contradictions And Limitations
The algorithm cannot handle fractional stoichiometric coefficients. Metabolites with connectivity larger than 40 were eliminated. The E-Coli network was reduced to 1005 reactions and 560 metabolites. The structural jumps in flux distributions are uncertain. The knock-out analysis assumed independent reactions. The independence assumption ignores shared enzymes. The exact scaling analysis was not possible. The maximum fluxes were assumed equal to 1. The knock-out reduction was set to 0.25 of the original value. The maximum flux was kept constant except for the knockout.

Claims
The proposed algorithm efficiently estimates the size and shape of the solution space of metabolic networks. The algorithm computes volume in polynomial time. The method is efficient on large biological systems. The results match exact algorithms. The method is compatible with Monte Carlo estimates. The algorithm cannot handle fractional stoichiometric coefficients. The exact scaling analysis was not possible. The method enables analysis of large metabolic networks. The approach can be extended to non-linear constraints. The method complements FBA and MOMA.
Low-redundancy reactions have a disproportionate impact on the size of the solution space upon knock-out. Most reactions have ∆S > −3 with little impact. A relevant fraction has ∆S < −3. Most high-impact reactions are in glycolysis. Reactions with little redundancy have more impact. Some high-impact reactions are in the Krebs cycle. The correlations show two regimes with a threshold. The metabolic capacities are highly affected by knock-outs. The results explain the impact of gene knock-outs. The correlations link flux distributions to knock-out effects.
The algorithm scales to large networks where exact methods fail. The algorithm keeps polynomial behavior at large sizes. Exact algorithms increase more than exponentially. The algorithm handles networks 50 times larger. The exact scaling analysis was not possible. The toy models were limited to N = 12. The method enables analysis of real-world networks. The algorithm is efficient on large biological systems. The method is applicable to systems biology.

Data And Code Availability
The stoichiometric matrix was extracted from [8]. The E-Coli network was extracted from [11].

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The algorithm was tested on toy models. The algorithm was tested on the Red Blood Cell network. The algorithm was tested on the E-Coli network. The metabolites with connectivity larger than 40 were eliminated. The reactions with fractional stoichiometric indexes were eliminated. The cofactors were removed except ATP and ADP. The network was reduced to 40 metabolites and 74 internal reactions. The external fluxes were considered irreversible.

Ethical Considerations
The authors equally contributed to this work.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1.1 displays the running time of LRS and BP. Figure 1.2 shows the effect of discretization on BP quality. Figure 1.3 shows the flux distributions of the Red Blood Cell network. Figure 1.4 shows the pdf of the average fluxes of the E-Coli network. Figure 1.5 shows the integrated distribution function of the average fluxes. Figure 1.6 shows the changes in S for the different reaction knock-outs. Figure 1.7 shows the correlations between entropy changes and flux values.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution: a novel, efficient algorithm for estimating the size and shape of the solution space of metabolic networks. 2. The strongest evidence: the algorithm matches exact and Monte Carlo results while scaling to large networks. 3. The future path: extending the approach to non-linear constraints and more general functional forms.

summary.title: Impact of Chronic Total Occlusion Lesion Length on Six-month Angiographic and 2-year Clinical Outcomes
summary.authors: Jihun Ahn; Byounggeol Choi; Yeon Choi; Jae Kyeong Byun; Ahmed Mashaly; Kareem Abdelshafi; Yoonjee Park; Young Jang; Woohyeun Kim; Eunjin Park; Jin Oh Na; Cheol Ung Choi; Eungju Kim; Chang Gyu Park; Hongseog Seo; Dongjoo Oh; Jinsu Byeon; Sangho Park; Hyeyon Yu; Seung-Woon W Rha
summary.field_subfield: Cardiovascular medicine / interventional cardiology
summary.executive_summary: This study investigated whether the length of a chronic total occlusion (CTO) lesion influences angiographic and clinical outcomes after successful percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with drug-eluting stents (DES). A total of 235 consecutive patients who underwent successful CTO PCI with DES between November 2004 and October 2010 at Korea University Guro Hospital were divided into a long CTO group (angiographic lesion length ≥30mm, n=159) and a short CTO group (angiographic lesion length <30mm, n=76). Baseline characteristics were largely similar, with prior PCI more frequent in the long CTO group and bifurcation lesions more frequent in the short CTO group. In-hospital complications were comparable except for a higher incidence of significant intimal dissection in the long CTO group. At six months, angiographic outcomes were similar between the two groups, including binary restenosis, in-stent restenosis, and late loss, although there was a numerically higher trend toward binary restenosis in the long CTO group (19.1% vs. 8.8%, p=0.12). Over two years, the incidence of total death (3.1% vs. 5.2%, p=0.43), cardiac death (1.2% vs. 2.6%, p=0.45), myocardial infarction (1.8% vs. 2.6%, p=0.71), and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) (21.3% vs. 13.1%, p=0.13) did not differ significantly between the groups. However, the incidence of repeat PCI (18.8% vs. 7.8%, p<0.05) and target vessel revascularization (TVR) (16.3% vs. 6.5%, p<0.05) was significantly higher in the long CTO group. Multivariate analysis identified long CTO as an independent predictor of repeat PCI (OR 4.26, CI 1.53-11.9, p=0.006) and TVR (OR 4.23, CI 1.52-11.8, p<0.05). The authors concluded that, despite successful CTO PCI with DES, long CTO lesions are associated with a higher rate of repeat revascularization, though this did not translate into differences in hard clinical endpoints such as mortality or cardiac death. The study acknowledges limitations including its non-randomized, single-center design, relatively small sample size, lack of routine follow-up angiography, and insufficient follow-up duration. These findings suggest that while long CTO lesions carry a higher risk of repeat revascularization, the overall safety and long-term clinical outcomes remain comparable to those of short CTO lesions, supporting the notion that procedural success with DES does not guarantee improved outcomes in long CTO disease. The authors emphasize the need for larger, long-term studies to draw definitive conclusions. This work contributes to the understanding of lesion-length-specific outcomes in the DES era and highlights the importance of considering baseline lesion characteristics when predicting clinical outcomes after CTO PCI. The results have implications for patient counseling, procedural planning, and the potential need for more aggressive surveillance or intervention strategies in patients with long CTO lesions. Overall, the study provides valuable insights into the nuanced relationship between CTO lesion length and clinical outcomes, while acknowledging the limitations of its observational design and the need for further research to confirm its findings. The findings also underscore the complexity of CTO disease and the challenges of predicting long-term outcomes based on lesion characteristics alone. By comparing angiographic and clinical outcomes between long and short CTO lesions, the study offers a comprehensive evaluation of the impact of lesion length on the success and durability of CTO PCI. Research Context
Drug-eluting stents have reduced restenosis and adverse events after PCI. Long coronary lesions remain a worse prognostic factor after PCI. CTO PCI success rates remain lower than non-CTO PCI. Long-term CTO outcomes depend on clinical risk factors and baseline lesion characteristics. No definitive answers exist for CTO outcomes according to lesion length in the DES era.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to investigate whether CTO lesion length impacts six-month angiographic and two-year clinical outcomes. The authors hypothesized that adverse clinical and angiographic outcomes would be more frequent in the long CTO group. Long CTO lesions were expected to have worse clinical risk factors such as prior MI and PCI. Newer-generation DES use was expected to be more common in the short CTO group. Long CTO was predicted to be an independent predictor of repeat PCI.

Methodological Details
The study enrolled 235 consecutive CTO patients who underwent successful PCI with DES. Patients were enrolled from November 2004 to October 2010 at Korea University Guro Hospital. Patients were divided into long CTO (≥30mm) and short CTO (<30mm) groups. The long CTO group comprised 159 patients and the short CTO group comprised 76 patients. The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board at Korea University Guro Hospital. All patients provided informed consent to participate in the study. CTO was defined as complete obstruction with TIMI flow grade 0 and duration ≥3 months. Only de novo lesions were included, and CTO due to in-stent restenosis was excluded. Loading doses of clopidogrel (300-600mg) and aspirin (200-300mg) were administered before the procedure. Maintenance therapy included aspirin (100mg) and clopidogrel (75mg) as dual antiplatelet therapy. Clopidogrel was encouraged to continue for at least one year. Cilostazol was administered by 200mg post-loading and then 100mg twice a day for at least one month.

Procedures And Architectures
PCI procedures were performed using current guidelines with standard techniques. Various guidewires were used to cross the CTO lesion. Atheroablative devices were not utilized; simple balloon pre-dilation was mostly performed. All PCI was performed using DES, with stent type decided by the operator. Procedural success was defined as final diameter stenosis <30% and TIMI grade ≥2. QCA parameters were measured before PCI, immediately after PCI, and 6 months after the procedure. The primary angiographic endpoint was binary restenosis at 6-12 months. Secondary angiographic endpoints included ISR, mean DS, MLD, and late loss at 6 months. Follow-up data were collected at two years via interview, medical record review, and/or telephone contact. The primary clinical endpoint was MACE, defined as total death, recurrent MI, and revascularization. Secondary clinical endpoints included death, MI, repeat PCI, TLR, TVR, and non-TVR. Continuous variables were analyzed with Student's t-test, and categorical variables with χ2 or Fisher's exact test.

Key Results
The long CTO group comprised 159 patients and the short CTO group comprised 76 patients. Prior PCI was more frequent in the long CTO group. Bifurcation lesions were more frequent in the short CTO group. Intimal dissection was more frequent in the long CTO group. In-hospital complications were similar between the two groups except for intimal dissection. Six-month angiographic outcomes were similar between the two groups. The incidence of binary restenosis was 19.1% vs. 8.8% (p=0.12) between the long and short CTO groups. The incidence of ISR was 33.3% vs. 26.6% (p=0.42) between the long and short CTO groups. The incidence of late loss was 0.65 ± 0.82 mm vs. 0.46 ± 0.56 mm (p=0.13) between the long and short CTO groups. Total death was 3.1% vs. 5.2% (p=0.43) between the long and short CTO groups. Cardiac death was 1.2% vs. 2.6% (p=0.45) between the long and short CTO groups. The incidence of MI was 1.8% vs. 2.6% (p=0.71) between the long and short CTO groups.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Long CTO lesions carry worse clinical risk factors such as prior MI and PCI. The higher incidence of repeat PCI and TVR in the long CTO group did not translate into differences in hard endpoints. The presence of less myocardial viability and collateral channels may lessen the harmful effects of restenosis. Long CTO was an independent predictor of repeat PCI with an OR of 4.26. Long CTO was an independent predictor of TVR with an OR of 4.23.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study is not a randomized study and is a single-center registry. Baseline clinical, lesion, and procedural characteristics were slightly different between the two groups. Follow-up coronary angiography was not routinely performed in all patients. The sample size was relatively small, limiting the power to detect differences in angiographic events. The two-year follow-up period was not long enough to evaluate long-term safety and efficacy.

Claims
Long CTO lesions are associated with a higher incidence of repeat PCI and TVR, but not with differences in hard clinical endpoints such as mortality or cardiac death. The incidence of repeat PCI was 18.8% vs. 7.8% (p<0.05) between the long and short CTO groups. The incidence of TVR was 16.3% vs. 6.5% (p<0.05) between the long and short CTO groups. Long CTO was an independent predictor of repeat PCI with an OR of 4.26. Long CTO was an independent predictor of TVR with an OR of 4.23. Total death was 3.1% vs. 5.2% (p=0.43) between the long and short CTO groups. Cardiac death was 1.2% vs. 2.6% (p=0.45) between the long and short CTO groups. The incidence of MACE was 21.3% vs. 13.1% (p=0.13) between the long and short CTO groups. The higher incidence of TVR in the long CTO group did not translate into differences in hard endpoints. PCI in the long CTO lesion with DES is similarly safe as compared with CTO PCI in the short CTO lesion. Long-term studies with larger populations are needed to draw definitive conclusions.
Successful CTO PCI with DES is associated with improved clinical outcomes compared with failed CTO PCI, including reduced rates of CABG. Successful CTO PCI was associated with reduced rates of CABG compared with failed CTO PCI. The incidence of MACE was 21.3% vs. 13.1% (p=0.13) between the long and short CTO groups. The safety profile, mid-term angiographic and long-term clinical outcomes were similar between the long CTO and the short CTO group.

Data And Code Availability
The study data were collected prospectively from a single-center registry.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study used strict statistical adjustment for risk factors such as sex, age, hypertension, DM, CKD, prior PCI, and bifurcation lesion. There could be unmeasured confounders and analytical bias despite strict statistical adjustment.

Ethical Considerations
The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board at Korea University Guro Hospital. All patients provided informed consent to participate in the study.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 demonstrated baseline clinical and angiographic characteristics. Table 2 demonstrated procedural and in-hospital complications. Table 3 summarized clinical outcomes for the 2-year follow-up period. Table 4 showed the predictors for repeat PCI and TVR. Table 5 demonstrated six-month angiographic outcomes.

Three Takeaways
The core contribution is that long CTO lesions are associated with a higher incidence of repeat PCI and TVR, but not with differences in hard clinical endpoints. The strongest evidence is the multivariate analysis showing long CTO as an independent predictor of repeat PCI (OR 4.26) and TVR (OR 4.23). The future path is to conduct long-term studies with larger populations to draw definitive conclusions.

summary.title: Frustration-driven successive metamagnetic transitions in TbB4
summary.authors: T. Inami, K. Ohwada, Y. H. Matsuda, Z. W. Ouyang, H. Nojiri, D. Okuyama, T. Matsumura, and Y. Murakami
summary.field_subfield: Condensed matter physics; magnetism of frustrated rare-earth compounds
summary.executive_summary: This letter reports resonant magnetic x-ray diffraction (RMXD) experiments on the Shastry-Sutherland-lattice compound TbB4, performed under strong pulsed magnetic fields up to 29 T. The material has two magnetic transition temperatures, TN1 = 44 K and TN2 = 22 K, and below TN2 its magnetic moments are confined to the basal ab-plane with additional in-plane anisotropy orienting them along the diagonal. For an XY-type magnet, one would anticipate a linear magnetization process when the field is applied along the c-axis, yet TbB4 instead exhibits a multi-step metamagnetic behavior between 16 and 28 T, with a reported 9 steps and a prominent one-half magnetization plateau. The authors argue that this curve is difficult to predict because TbB4 has an XY-type ground state. The central experimental advance is the observation of the 100 magnetic reflection intensity as a function of field. The net diffraction intensity of the 100 reflection is about 2x10^5 counts/s, marginally strong enough for a pulsed-field experiment. Two key outcomes emerge: first, a considerable amount of the 100 reflection intensity remains in the magnetization plateau phases above 16 T, decreasing with increasing field above 16 T and staying constant between 20 and 24 T, where the one-half plateau is observed; second, the characteristic polarization dependence of RMXD shows that the observed large (1,0,0) component in the plateau phases consists of ab-plane components rather than the c-axis component. The one-half plateau is clearly reproduced, and the diffracted intensity of the corresponding structure is about one-quarter of the ground state, broadly consistent with the observed intensity of about 30-50% of the intensity at 0 T. Similar results were obtained with other parameter sets and cell sizes (2x2 and 1x3 cells). The authors propose that frustration is the key to understanding the observed multi-step magnetization, because frustration lifts the degeneracy at the critical fields and creates the successive metamagnetic transitions. The paper emphasizes the integration of RMXD using brilliant third-generation synchrotron radiation and excellent pulsed-magnetic-field techniques, which enables exploration of magnetic structures at high fields close to 30 T.
