documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This letter reports resonant magnetic x-ray diffraction (RMXD) experiments on the Shastry-Sutherland-lattice compound TbB4, performed under strong pulsed magnetic fields up to 29 T. TbB4 is a rare-earth tetra-boride that crystallizes in the tetragonal space group P4/mbm and whose rare-earth network is equivalent to the geometrically frustrated Shastry-Sutherland lattice. The material has two magnetic transition temperatures, TN1 = 44 K and TN2 = 22 K, and below TN2 its magnetic moments are confined to the basal ab-plane with additional in-plane anisotropy orienting them along the diagonal. For an XY-type magnet, one would anticipate a linear magnetization process when the field is applied along the c-axis, yet TbB4 instead exhibits a multi-step metamagnetic behavior between 16 and 28 T, with a reported 9 steps and a prominent one-half magnetization plateau. The authors argue that this curve is difficult to predict because TbB4 has an XY-type ground state. The central experimental advance is the observation of the 100 magnetic reflection intensity as a function of field. The net diffraction intensity of the 100 reflection is about 2x10^5 counts/s, marginally strong enough for a pulsed-field experiment. Two key outcomes emerge: first, a considerable amount of the 100 reflection intensity remains in the magnetization plateau phases above 16 T, decreasing with increasing field above 16 T and staying constant between 20 and 24 T, where the one-half plateau is observed; second, the characteristic polarization dependence of RMXD shows that the observed large (1,0,0) component in the plateau phases consists of ab-plane components rather than the c-axis component. This is surprising because plateau phases are usually expected to have collinear structures with no ordered moment perpendicular to the field. From these data, the authors deduce a simple spin model in which the ground state is a very hard XY spin with in-plane anisotropy E and the excited state is an Ising spin with energy gap D, and they calculate the magnetization curve. The one-half plateau is clearly reproduced, and the diffracted intensity of the corresponding structure is about one-quarter of the ground state, broadly consistent with the observed intensity of about 30-50% of the intensity at 0 T. Similar results were obtained with other parameter sets and cell sizes (2x2 and 1x3 cells). The authors propose that frustration is the key to understanding the observed multi-step magnetization, because frustration lifts the degeneracy at the critical fields and creates the successive metamagnetic transitions. The paper emphasizes the integration of RMXD using brilliant third-generation synchrotron radiation and excellent pulsed-magnetic-field techniques, which enables exploration of magnetic structures at high fields close to 30 T.

Research Context
Magnetization plateaus are a hallmark of several magnetic materials, arising from mechanisms such as zero compressibility and Sz being a good quantum number. Ising-type antiferromagnets with competing J1 and J2 interactions are the most comprehensible class, producing step-like magnetization curves. Examples of Ising-type plateaus include the one-third plateau of CoCl2·2H2O and the multi-step curves of PrCo2Si2 and CeSb. Magnetization plateaus also occur for Heisenberg spins, including isolated dimers and orthogonally connected dimer systems. Geometrically frustrated Heisenberg antiferromagnets such as triangular- and pyrochlore-lattice systems exhibit one-third and one-half plateaus. A crucial point is that all plateau phases have a collinear magnetic structure with no ordered moment perpendicular to the field. TbB4 was recently found to exhibit a multi-step magnetization curve that resembles none of the previously known magnets. To the authors' best knowledge, CsFeCl3 is considered to be the only example of a magnet with ordered perpendicular components in the plateau phase. In these perpendicular-component magnets, frustration plays a central role in the multi-step magnetization process.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is why TbB4 exhibits a multi-step magnetization process that is hardly predicted for an XY-type ground state. The authors hypothesize that the plateau phases are accompanied by large XY components of magnetic moments, contrary to the usual collinear expectation. The authors predict that the observed large (1,0,0) component in the plateau phases consists of ab-plane components rather than the c-axis component. The authors hypothesize that a simple spin model with a very hard XY ground state and excited Ising spins can reproduce the magnetization curve. The authors predict that frustration lifts the degeneracy at the critical fields and creates the observed multi-step metamagnetic behavior. The authors predict that the one-half plateau is clearly reproduced by the model, with a diffracted intensity of about one-quarter of the ground state. The authors predict that the critical field of the one-third plateau phase is inevitably smaller than that of the one-half plateau phase. The authors predict that the proposed model captures basic features of the real TbB4 despite being simplified.

Methodological Details
The study used single crystals of TbB4 grown by the floating zone method. The experiments were carried out at undulator beamline BL22XU at SPring-8. The x-ray energy was tuned to the Tb LIII absorption edge at 7.514 keV. Magnetic fields up to 29 T were generated using a small pulsed magnet with a 0.6 ms pulse duration. The magnet is a split-pair with two windows prepared for incoming and outgoing x-rays. The magnet and sample were attached to the cold head of a conventional closed cycle refrigerator. A high-counting-rate detector, an avalanche photodiode, was used with a typical resolution of 10 µs. The scattering plane was horizontal with the a* axis in the plane, and magnetic fields were vertical and parallel to the c-axis. The field strength was monitored as a function of time to obtain the field dependence of the diffraction intensity. The sample surface was locally heated by irradiation of synchrotron x-rays, and the true sample temperature was estimated by measuring the temperature dependence of the magnetic peak intensity. The data for the field dependence of the 100 reflection at 18 K were an average of 30 field-scans. The net diffraction intensity of the 100 reflection is about 2x10^5 counts/s, marginally strong enough for a pulsed-field experiment.

Procedures And Architectures
The spin Hamiltonian includes XY interactions, Ising interactions, in-plane anisotropy E, energy gap D, and the Zeeman term. The spins are treated as unit vectors in the Hamiltonian. Magnetization curves were calculated for finite-size cells with periodic boundary conditions. The authors consider 4 spins in the crystallographic unit cell (1x1 cell). For simplicity, the authors initially consider the limit E →∞, so each spin has only 4 states. The authors took J1 = 2, J2 = 1, J3 = 2, D = 1 for the calculations. The calculated magnetization curve is shown in Fig. 4(a), and the one-half magnetization plateau is clearly reproduced. Similar results were obtained with other sets of parameters and different cell sizes (2x2 and 1x3 cells). The authors set the in-plane anisotropy E finite to allow moments to rotate in the ab-plane, treating Ising sites as defects. The authors note that interactions further than J3 must be included to account for the splitting at Hc1.

Key Results
The 100 reflection intensity remains in the magnetization plateau phases above 16 T, decreasing with increasing field and staying constant between 20 and 24 T. The constant intensity between 20 and 24 T corresponds to the one-half magnetization plateau phase. The plateau phases include the (1,0,0) component in their magnetic structures. The observed large (1,0,0) component in the plateau phases consists of the ab-plane components rather than the c-axis component. The diffracted intensity of the one-half plateau structure is about one-quarter of the ground state. The diffracted intensity is broadly consistent with the observed intensity of about 30-50% of the intensity at 0 T. The one-half magnetization plateau is clearly reproduced by the model. The critical field of the one-third plateau phase is inevitably smaller than that of the one-half plateau phase. Many states are degenerate at the critical fields Hc1/2 and Hc1 when E=∞. The magnetic intensity observed in the plateau phases illustrates that large XY-components of the magnetic moments coexist with aligned Z-components. The magnetic moments in the one-third plateau phase are rearranged to reduce the total energy. The resultant magnetic lattice of the one-half plateau phase is not frustrated, as illustrated by collinear in-plane components.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The plateau phases have large XY components of magnetic moments, contrary to the usual collinear expectation. A canted magnetic structure would result in a continuous magnetization curve unlike the observed step-like process. The plateau phases consist of very hard XY-type magnetic moments and Ising-like magnetic moments. Frustration lifts the degeneracy at the critical fields and creates the observed multi-step metamagnetic behavior. Frustration is not only an origin of degenerate states, but also breaks degeneracy. The basic scenario that frustration lifts the degeneracy at a metamagnetic transition is common for both TbB4 and CsFeCl3. Frustration-driven successive metamagnetic transitions are a general mechanism. The proposed spin model captures basic features of the real TbB4 despite being simplified.

Contradictions And Limitations
The proposed spin model is very much simplified, with no cross-term between the XY and Ising spins. The model is a simplification, but the authors believe it captures basic features of the real TbB4. The authors acknowledge that the spin models for TbB4 and CsFeCl3 are quite different. The degeneracy at the critical fields is a normal phenomenon, but if this degeneracy is lifted, the multi-step magnetization curve can be reproduced. The proposed model is a hypothesis that requires further validation. The one-half plateau is reproduced, but the one-third plateau is only proposed as a possible magnetic structure. The sample surface was locally heated by irradiation of synchrotron x-rays, which could affect the measurements. The net diffraction intensity of the 100 reflection is marginally strong enough for a pulsed-field experiment.

Claims
The plateau phases of TbB4 have large XY components of magnetic moments, contrary to the usual collinear expectation. The 100 reflection intensity remains in the plateau phases above 16 T. The observed large (1,0,0) component in the plateau phases consists of the ab-plane components. The magnetic intensity illustrates that large XY-components coexist with aligned Z-components. A canted magnetic structure would result in a continuous magnetization curve unlike the observed step-like process. It is expected that all magnetic moments in plateau phases are parallel or antiparallel to the field. The plateau phases consist of very hard XY-type magnetic moments and Ising-like magnetic moments. Frustration plays a central role in the multi-step magnetization process.
Frustration is the key to understanding the observed multi-step magnetization, lifting the degeneracy at the critical fields. The frustrated nature of the SS lattice lifts the degeneracy at the critical fields. The basic scenario that frustration lifts the degeneracy at a metamagnetic transition is common for both magnets. Frustration-driven successive metamagnetic transitions are a general mechanism. Classical continuous spins on the SS lattice are not frustrated in the strict sense. The degeneracy at the critical fields is a normal phenomenon observed in metamagnetic transitions. Frustration is not only an origin of degenerate states, but also breaks degeneracy. The proposed spin model captures basic features of the real TbB4.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Similar results were obtained with other sets of parameters and different cell sizes (2x2 and 1x3 cells). The one-half plateau is reproduced with the limit E →∞, and the model is simplified.

Key Figures Tables
Fig. 1 shows examples of magnetization plateaus: ground states (left) and magnetization plateau phases (right). Fig. 2(a) shows the magnetic structure of TbB4 between TN1 and TN2, and Fig. 2(b) shows the magnetization process. Fig. 3(a) shows the incident energy dependence of the 100 reflection, Fig. 3(b) shows the temperature dependence, and Fig. 3(c) shows the field dependence. Fig. 4(a) shows the calculated magnetization curve for E →∞, Fig. 4(b) shows a possible magnetic structure of the one-third plateau phase, and Fig. 4(c) shows the schematic energy diagram.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the demonstration that TbB4 has large XY components of magnetic moments in the plateau phases, revealing a new class of frustrated magnets. 2. The strongest evidence is the observation that the observed large (1,0,0) component in the plateau phases consists of the ab-plane components. 3. The future path is the application of RMXD and pulsed-magnetic-field techniques to explore magnetic structures at high fields close to 30 T.

summary.title: Three-dimensional topological valley photonics
summary.authors: Wenhao Li, Qiaolu Chen, Ning Han, Xinrui Li, Fujia Chen, Junyao Wu, Yuang Pan, Yudong Ren, Hongsheng Chen, Haoran Xue, Yihao Yang
summary.field_subfield: Photonics / Topological photonics (physics of light)
summary.executive_summary: Topological valley photonics exploits the valley degree of freedom to control electromagnetic waves, but prior work has been confined to two dimensions, where photonic confinement along the third dimension is usually achieved in a non-topological way such as total internal reflection. Such 2D systems support single-polarization valley states, suffer from out-of-plane losses, and can only manipulate light flow in planar geometries. Full confinement and full control of light flow require a complete photonic bandgap, in which light of any polarization is forbidden to propagate in any direction in three dimensions, and this remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces a theoretical and experimental framework of three-dimensional (3D) topological valley photonics with a complete photonic bandgap and vectorial valley-contrasting physics. The 3D valley systems exhibit triple pairs of valleys characterized by valley Chern vectors, enabling vectorial bulk valley vortices and canalized chiral valley surface states. The valley Chern vectors and the circulating propagation direction of the valley surface states are intrinsically governed by the right-hand-thumb rule. The authors use a 3D photonic crystal with lattice constant a = 20 mm, built from perfect electric conductor spheres and rods, and break inversion symmetry by setting D1 = 6.4 mm and D2 = 3.6 mm to open a complete bandgap. They verify vectorial valley-contrasting Berry curvature using a vectorial chiral source array and pump-probe measurements, and demonstrate robust canalized valley surface states on all surfaces of a shaped sample. The measured outcoupling directions at 13.8 GHz are −32.9°, 0°, and +32.9°, corresponding to Wy−, X, and Wy+. The surface states propagate diffractionlessly along +y corresponding to the Wx− valley, and the right-hand-thumb rule is confirmed across (001) and (010) surfaces. The findings highlight applications in 3D waveguiding, directional radiation, and imaging, and suggest extension to terahertz and optical ranges.

The findings highlight applications in 3D waveguiding, directional radiation, and imaging, and suggest extension to terahertz and optical ranges.

Research Context
Valley photonics supplements conventional degrees of freedom to control light. 2D valley photonic crystals host a single pair of valleys with scalar invariants. Valley-contrasting physics underlies vortex states and edge states. VPCs are experimentally feasible without breaking time-reversal symmetry. Prior valley photonics is limited to two dimensions. 2D systems suffer from out-of-plane losses and planar confinement. Full confinement requires a complete photonic bandgap. A complete bandgap remains a significant challenge.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can 3D topological valley photonics be realized with a complete bandgap? Do 3D valley systems exhibit triple pairs of valleys with vectorial invariants? Are valley Chern vectors the governing vectorial invariant? Do vectorial bulk valley vortices and canalized chiral surface states arise? Is the propagation governed by the right-hand-thumb rule? Can valley surface states be canalized on all sample surfaces? Can valley states be selectively excited by chirality-matched sources?

Methodological Details
The study is both theoretical and experimental. The 3D photonic crystal has lattice constant a = 20 mm. Lattice vectors are a1 = (a/2, a/2, 0), a2 = (0, a/2, a/2), a3 = (a/2, 0, a/2). The crystal is a photonic diamond with PEC spheres and rods. Each fcc cell contains two spheres with diameters D1 and D2. Nearest spheres are connected by PEC rods with diameter B1 = 2.4 mm. Next-nearest spheres are connected by PEC rods with diameter B2 = 1.2 mm. B2 rods suppress high-order modes for a clean bandstructure. Inversion symmetry is preserved when D1 = D2 = 5 mm. Inversion symmetry is broken when D1 = 6.4 mm and D2 = 3.6 mm. The broken symmetry gaps out nodal lines to form a complete bandgap. The six valleys are located at Wx±, Wy±, and Wz±.

Procedures And Architectures
The band structure is computed and shown in Fig. 1(b). Nodal chains form along Wα±-X when ∆D = 0. The valley momenta are (±π/a, 2π/a, 0), (0, ±π/a, 2π/a), and (2π/a, 0, ±π/a). The effective Hamiltonian is derived by the k · p method. The mass term is m = (ω1 − ω2)/2 from broken inversion symmetry. The vectorial chiral source array uses four sources. Source positions are (0, 0, 0), (−a/2, −a/2, 0), (−a/2, 0, −a/2), and (0, −a/2, −a/2). Phase delays are (0, π/2, π, 3π/2) for Wy− and (0, −π/2, −π, −3π/2) for Wy+. The valley Chern vector is integrated over a planar region around each valley. The VCVs are (±1/2, 0, 0), (0, ±1/2, 0), and (0, 0, ±1/2). The boundary condition uses τz = σy sin θV + σz cos θV. The surface is covered by a metallic plate with perforations of interval a/2.

Key Results
The Berry curvature has nonzero component only in the kx-ky plane. The measured outcoupling directions at 13.8 GHz are −32.9°, 0°, and +32.9°. The clockwise and counterclockwise windings correspond to −32.9° and +32.9°. The no-winding case corresponds to 0° at X. The radiated beams are single-directional in 3D space. The VCVs are (±1/2, 0, 0), (0, ±1/2, 0), and (0, 0, ±1/2). The surface states traverse the bandgap with linear dispersion. The surface transmission stays high within the complete bandgap. The surface states propagate canalization along +y for the Wx− valley. The isofrequency contours are flat, confirmed experimentally and numerically. The surface states exist on all (100), (010), and (001) surfaces. The propagation direction is locked to each valley without intervalley scattering.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The vectorial nature of 3D valley states is revealed. The valley Chern vectors and propagation direction obey the right-hand-thumb rule. The rule is an intrinsic relation determined by the bulk Hamiltonian. The canalization is an intrinsic property of the surface states. The surface states offer opportunities for imaging and lensing. The orbital moments provide a means to control the angular momentum of light. The directional outcoupling can create narrow-beam antennae. The concept can be extended to terahertz and optical ranges.

Contradictions And Limitations
The demonstration is at lower frequencies. The concept can be extended to higher frequencies. The exact operating frequency is not uniformly stated across figures. The sample shape is required for surface states on all surfaces. The boundary condition relies on tuning D3 and h. The random seed and train/test split are not applicable to this physics study.

Claims
3D topological valley photonics with a complete photonic bandgap and vectorial valley-contrasting physics is realized. The framework is both theoretical and experimental. The complete bandgap forbids propagation of any polarization in 3D. The 3D systems exhibit triple pairs of valleys. The Berry curvature has nonzero component only in the kx-ky plane. Prior valley photonics is limited to 2D systems. 2D systems suffer from out-of-plane losses. The concept can be extended to terahertz and optical ranges. The framework enables 3D waveguiding, directional radiation, and imaging.
Vectorial valley-contrasting Berry curvature enables selective excitation of chiral valley states. The vectorial chiral source array uses four sources. The measured outcoupling directions are −32.9°, 0°, and +32.9°. The radiated beams are single-directional in 3D space. The 2D radiation pattern diverges in the vertical direction. The directional outcoupling can serve as a mechanism for narrow-beam antennae.
Robust canalized chiral valley surface states exist on all sample surfaces. The surface states exist on all (100), (010), and (001) surfaces. The surface states propagate canalization along +y for the Wx− valley. The isofrequency contours are flat, confirmed experimentally and numerically. Existing 3D topological photonic insulators support surface states on certain surfaces only. The canalization offers opportunities for imaging and lensing.
The right-hand-thumb rule relates valley Chern vectors to the circulating direction of valley surface states. The rule is confirmed across (001) and (010) surfaces. The rule is an intrinsic relation determined by the bulk Hamiltonian. The propagation direction is locked to each valley without intervalley scattering. The exact operating frequency is not uniformly stated across figures. The rule enables valley conservation through sharp corners.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The B2 rods suppress high-order modes for a clean bandstructure. The boundary condition is satisfied when h = 6.25 mm and D3 = 4 mm. The canalization is confirmed both experimentally and numerically. The valley-locking property is revealed experimentally.

Key Figures Tables
Fig. 1 shows the 3D VPC, band structure, valleys, and Berry curvature. Fig. 2 shows selective excitation of vectorial valley states. Fig. 3 shows canalized chiral valley surface states. Fig. 4 shows the right-hand-thumb rule relating VCVs and surface states.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a 3D topological valley photonics framework with a complete bandgap and vectorial valley-contrasting physics. 2. The strongest evidence is the canalized chiral valley surface states on all surfaces obeying the right-hand-thumb rule. 3. The future path is extending the concept to terahertz and optical ranges with all-dielectric crystals.

summary.title: Stable open-shell aromatic nitric acid radicals: accessing highly efficient photothermal conversion with restricted radiative decay
summary.authors: Zejun Wang; Jiawen Zhou; Yiheng Zhang; Weiya Zhu; Yuan Li
summary.field_subfield: Organic photothermal materials / radical chemistry / solar-driven water evaporation
summary.type_of_paper: Experimental study (materials synthesis and photophysical/photothermal characterization)
summary.executive_summary: Open-shell organic radicals are usually unstable in air because of unsatisfied valency, but aromatic nitric acid radicals (ANARs) are stabilized by rich resonance structures that delocalize the unpaired electron over a conjugated backbone. This work reports a series of star-shaped ANARs prepared by demethylation and air oxidation of phenolic hydroxyl precursors. The materials show high spin concentration and strongly enhanced nonradiative decay, which favors photothermal conversion. The best performer, TPA-TPA-O6, reaches a solar-to-vapor efficiency of 89.41% and a water evaporation rate of 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ under 1 sun, with negligible photobleaching and excellent stability, including seawater desalination. The study positions stable organic small-molecule radicals as a low-cost, reproducible, and heavy-metal-free alternative to inorganic and polymeric photothermal materials.

claims.description: Stable open-shell aromatic nitric acid radicals are efficient, stable, and low-cost photothermal materials.
High spin concentration and restricted radiative decay drive photothermal conversion.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
Open-shell organic radicals are usually unstable in air because of unsatisfied valency, but aromatic nitric acid radicals (ANARs) are stabilized by rich resonance structures that delocalize the unpaired electron over a conjugated backbone. This work reports a series of star-shaped ANARs prepared by demethylation and air oxidation of phenolic hydroxyl precursors. The materials show high spin concentration and strongly enhanced nonradiative decay, which favors photothermal conversion. The best performer, TPA-TPA-O6, reaches a solar-to-vapor efficiency of 89.41% and a water evaporation rate of 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ under 1 sun, with negligible photobleaching and excellent stability, including seawater desalination. The study positions stable organic small-molecule radicals as a low-cost, reproducible, and heavy-metal-free alternative to inorganic and polymeric photothermal materials.

Research Context
Open-shell radicals are usually unstable in air due to unsatisfied valency. Radicals are attractive for optoelectronics, magnets, photothermal, thermoelectric, and spintronics. Narrow optical band gaps can be tuned by chemical modification and structural control. Radical materials have good biocompatibility for photothermal and biological use. Organic small molecules are overlooked but avoid heavy-metal toxicity. Stable neutral radicals are rarely reported and hard to prepare. Airstable conjugated radicals are challenging due to high oxygen reactivity. Photothermal materials convert NIR light into heat via nonradiative decay.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can stable, heavy-metal-free organic small-molecule radicals serve as efficient photothermal materials? Do star-shaped aromatic nitric acid radicals combine stability with high photothermal performance? Will high spin concentration drive nonradiative decay and boost photothermal conversion? Will TPA-TPA-O6 outperform the other three cores in photothermal and stability? Will the radical platform enable efficient solar-driven water evaporation and desalination?

Methodological Details
Four star-shaped ANARs were synthesized with different cores. Materials were made by demethylation and air oxidation of phenolic precursors. Precursors were methoxy-substituted phenol derivatives. Synthesis used only two steps with high yield and easy purification. Structures were characterized in supporting information figures. UV-vis-NIR spectra were recorded in DMSO solution and film. Cyclic voltammetry used 0.1 M nBu4NPF6 in dichloromethane. CV scan rate was 0.1 V/s. Radicals were coated on carbon-glass electrodes to form films. Potentials were referenced to SCE with Fc+/Fc internal standard. HOMO/LUMO levels were derived from CV curves. ESR was used to measure spin concentration at 0.02 mmol.

Procedures And Architectures
Demethylation and oxidation generated the neutral radicals. PLQYs were measured in dichloromethane solution and film. HOMO levels of the four radicals were measured. Photothermal tests used an 808 nm laser at 0.8 W cm⁻². Temperature was monitored with an IR thermal camera. The interfacial evaporator used white PU porous foam. TPA-TPA-O6 was loaded by impregnation and drying at 80 °C. The foam had a 2.0 cm diameter with 30 mg loading. Evaporation was tested under 1 sun (1.0 kW m⁻²). Seawater desalination reduced four primary ions.

Key Results
TPA-TPA-O6 film showed a large red-shifted radical absorption. TPA-TPA-O6 powder was black, indicating wide visible absorption. TPA-PY-O8 and TPA-TPZ-O6 showed absorption edges near 1000 nm and 800 nm. All precursors fluoresced between 450 and 570 nm. Radicals had PLQY below 1%, confirming radical formation. TPA-TPA-O6 HOMO was -4.90 eV. TPA-TPA-O6 HOMO was enhanced versus its precursor. TPA-TPA-O6 and Spiro-O8 had enhanced ESR signal intensity. TPA-TPA-O6 PLQY was 0.1%. TPA-TPA-O6 PLQY was the most quenched in the solid state. TPA-TPA-O6 powder absorption spanned 300 to 2000 nm. TPA-TPA-O6 rose from 25 °C to ~210 °C in 60 s at 0.8 W cm⁻².

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
High spin concentration drives nonradiative decay and photothermal conversion. Restricted radiative decay favors photothermal performance. Strong donor-acceptor conjugation reduces bandgap and increases paramagnetism. TPA-TPA-O6 is the best due to wide NIR absorption and high paramagnetism. The design enables future organic electronic and spintronic applications.

Contradictions And Limitations
TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 showed poor photothermal performance.

Claims
Stable open-shell aromatic nitric acid radicals are efficient, stable, and low-cost photothermal materials. TPA-TPA-O6 reached 89.41% solar-to-vapor efficiency. TPA-TPA-O6 reached 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ evaporation rate. TPA-TPA-O6 showed negligible photobleaching. TPA-TPA-O6 was stable for ten laser cycles. TPA-TPA-O6 is a pure organic small molecule. TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 had low photothermal performance. TPA-TPA-O6 may be partially protonated. The platform enables solar-driven water evaporation and desalination. The platform enables future organic electronic and spintronic applications.
High spin concentration and restricted radiative decay drive photothermal conversion. High spin concentration leads to nonradiative decay. TPA-TPA-O6 had the lowest PLQY. TPA-TPA-O6 had the most quenched fluorescence. TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 had higher PLQY. TPA-TPA-O6 may be partially protonated. The design concept allows structural optimization. The design enables future organic electronic and spintronic applications.

Data And Code Availability
Supporting Information is available free of charge at the ACS link.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
TPA-TPA-O6 was stable for ten laser cycles. TPA-TPA-O6 temperature rose regularly with laser power. TPA-TPA-O6 recovered to ambient temperature after laser off. TPA-TPA-O6 was stable in powder and PU-dispersed states. TPA-TPA-O6 was stable in seawater desalination. TPA-TPA-O6 was cheap and easy to synthesize. TPA-TPA-O6 was soluble in green solvents. TPA-TPA-O6 had high reproducibility and solution processibility. TPA-TPA-O6 had competitive performance among organic materials. TPA-TPA-O6 had a simple synthesis with high yield. TPA-TPA-O6 had comparable performance with previous pure organic materials. TPA-TPA-O6 had a wide absorption spectrum.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 2A showed UV-vis spectra of TPA-TPA-OMe in solution and film. Figure 2B showed TPA-PY-OMe and TPA-TPZ-OMe absorption. Figure 2C showed TPA-PY-O8 and TPA-TPZ-O6 absorption. Figure 3 showed highly reversible CV curves. Figure 4A showed ESR spectra. Figure 4B showed PLQY emission between 450 and 570 nm. Figure 4C showed the interfacial evaporation system. Figure 4D showed photothermal conversion efficiency. Figure 5A showed rapid temperature rise to ~210 °C. Figure 5B showed the temperature change picture. Figure 5C showed temperature rise with laser power. Figure 6A showed photothermal conversion.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is stable open-shell aromatic nitric acid radicals as efficient photothermal materials. 2. The strongest evidence is 89.41% solar-to-vapor efficiency and 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ evaporation rate. 3. The future path is developing planar ANARs for photothermal, organic electronics, spintronics, and magnetic devices.

summary.title: Can giant planets form by gravitational fragmentation of discs? Radiative hydrodynamic simulations of the inner disc region
summary.authors: D. Stamatellos & A. P. Whitworth
summary.field_subfield: Astrophysics: planetary system formation / protoplanetary discs
summary.executive_summary: This paper investigates whether giant planets can form close to solar-type stars through gravitational fragmentation of protoplanetary discs. The authors perform radiative hydrodynamic simulations of the inner disc region (R < 40 AU) using the SPH code dragon, incorporating a newly developed method to treat the energy equation and equation of state, including radiative transfer effects, dust opacity changes, and the chemical/internal states of hydrogen and helium. Two cases are examined: (i) a disc heated only by an ambient background radiation field of 10 K, and (ii) a disc with additional heating from the central star (TBGR ∝ R−1). In both cases, the disc does not fragment. In the first case, the disc is Toomre unstable at ~30-35 AU but cannot cool fast enough (cooling time >~2tORB). In the second case, the disc cools fast enough but is not gravitationally unstable (Q >~1.5). The results corroborate earlier work by Boley et al. (2006) and Cai et al. (2007), despite using different radiative transfer treatments. The authors conclude that disc fragmentation is unlikely to produce giant planets around solar-type stars at radii <~50 AU. This work contributes to resolving contradictory results in the literature about disc fragmentation, which stem largely from different treatments of radiative transfer. The study uses 2×10^5 SPH particles and compares with analytic calculations of Hubeny (1990) for the vertical temperature profile. The findings have implications for understanding hot Jupiter formation, as fragmentation at large radii (>~100 AU) would produce objects unlikely to migrate inwards to become hot Jupiters.

claims.description: Disc fragmentation is unlikely to produce giant planets around solar-type stars at radii <~50 AU.
The results are consistent with previous simulations despite different radiative transfer treatments.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper investigates whether giant planets can form close to solar-type stars through gravitational fragmentation of protoplanetary discs. The authors perform radiative hydrodynamic simulations of the inner disc region (R < 40 AU) using the SPH code dragon, incorporating a newly developed method to treat the energy equation and equation of state, including radiative transfer effects, dust opacity changes, and the chemical/internal states of hydrogen and helium. Two cases are examined: (i) a disc heated only by an ambient background radiation field of 10 K, and (ii) a disc with additional heating from the central star (TBGR ∝ R−1). In both cases, the disc does not fragment. In the first case, the disc is Toomre unstable at ~30-35 AU but cannot cool fast enough (cooling time >~2tORB). In the second case, the disc cools fast enough but is not gravitationally unstable (Q >~1.5). The results corroborate earlier work by Boley et al. (2006) and Cai et al. (2007), despite using different radiative transfer treatments. The authors conclude that disc fragmentation is unlikely to produce giant planets around solar-type stars at radii <~50 AU. This work contributes to resolving contradictory results in the literature about disc fragmentation, which stem largely from different treatments of radiative transfer. The study uses 2×10^5 SPH particles and compares with analytic calculations of Hubeny (1990) for the vertical temperature profile. The findings have implications for understanding hot Jupiter formation, as fragmentation at large radii (>~100 AU) would produce objects unlikely to migrate inwards to become hot Jupiters.

Research Context
Disc fragmentation has been proposed as a mechanism for forming giant planets close to solar-type stars. Two main theories exist for giant planet formation: core accretion and gravitational fragmentation. Gravitational fragmentation requires the disc to be gravitationally unstable and to cool fast enough. The first condition is gravitational instability, quantified by the Toomre parameter Q <~1. The second condition is that the disc must cool on a dynamical timescale. Theoretical and simulation results on disc cooling are contradictory. Whether real discs satisfy these conditions remains uncertain. Hydrodynamic simulations have produced contradictory results due to different radiative transfer treatments.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether giant planets can form by gravitational fragmentation of discs in the inner region. The study focuses on the thermodynamics of discs and the probability of fragmentation. The authors hypothesize that fragmentation is unlikely in the inner disc region due to cooling or stability constraints. In the first case, the disc cannot cool fast enough to fragment. In the second case, the disc is not gravitationally unstable. The authors predict that fragmentation is possible at larger distances (>~100 AU) but not in the inner region. The predicted outcome is that gas giant planets probably cannot form close to the central star by gravitational fragmentation.

Methodological Details
The simulations use the SPH code dragon. The code uses an octal tree to compute gravity and find neighbours. The code uses adaptive smoothing lengths. The code uses multiple particle timesteps. The code uses artificial viscosity with α = 0.1 and β = 0.2. The code uses a second-order Runge-Kutta integration scheme. The energy equation is treated with the method of Stamatellos et al. (2007). The method accounts for compressional heating, viscous heating, radiation heating from the background, radiation cooling, and radiation heating from the particle's neighbourhood. The gas is assumed to be a mixture of hydrogen and helium. The equation of state accounts for rotational and vibrational degrees of freedom of molecular hydrogen. The equation of state accounts for different chemical states of hydrogen and helium. The effects of H2 dissociation, H0 ionisation, and the first and second ionisation of He are included.

Procedures And Architectures
The disc is simulated with a mass of 0.07 M⊙ around a 0.5 M⊙ star. The disc initially extends from 2 to 40 AU. The initial surface density follows Σ(R) ∼R−1/2. The initial temperature follows T(R) ∼R−1. The surface density profile is Σ(R) = Σ0 R−1/2 with Σ0 = 1.6 × 10^3 g cm−2. The temperature at R ≃1 AU is T0 = 1200 K. The asymptotic temperature far from the central star is T∞= 10 K. The simulations use 2×10^5 SPH particles. The first case uses a constant background radiation field of TBGR = 10 K. The second case uses radiation from the central star with TBGR ∝ R−1. The disc relaxes to a quasi-steady state within ~250 yr under low background heating. The vertical temperature profile is compared with the analytic calculations of Hubeny (1990).

Key Results
In the first case, the disc does not fragment because it cannot cool fast enough. The disc relaxes to a lower-temperature quasi-steady state when heating from the central star is ignored. The disc cools slowly under low background heating. Weak spiral arms form in the disc but they do not show any tendency to fragment. The disc is Toomre unstable at ~30-35 AU. The cooling time throughout the disc is generally >~2tORB. In the second case, the disc cools fast enough to fragment at radii >~20 AU. However, the disc does not fragment because it is not gravitationally unstable with Q >~1.5. The heating from the central star stabilizes the disc. The disc appears axisymmetric with no signs of spiral arms. The adiabatic index is γ = 5/3 outside ~10 AU where the temperature is less than ~80 K. Closer to the central star, γ = 7/5 due to the excitation of the rotational degrees of freedom of molecular hydrogen.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results corroborate the findings of Boley et al. (2006) and Cai et al. (2007). The agreement despite different radiative transfer treatments is reassuring. The cooling time being >~2tORB explains the lack of fragmentation in the first case. The lack of gravitational instability in the second case explains the lack of fragmentation. The findings suggest that fragmentation is possible at larger distances (>~100 AU) but not in the inner region. Fragmentation at large radii produces mostly brown dwarfs and occasionally low-mass hydrogen-burning stars or planetary-mass objects. Planetary-mass objects formed at large radii are unlikely to migrate inwards to become hot Jupiters. The findings have implications for understanding hot Jupiter formation.

Contradictions And Limitations
The temperatures in the simulations are not high enough for molecular hydrogen to dissociate. Contributions from metals are ignored. The mean molecular weight µ is constant. The results are limited to the inner region of discs (R < 40 AU). The conclusions are based on two cases only. The results are compared with previous simulations and analytic calculations. The study does not account for the effects of stellar irradiation in the first case. The study does not account for the effects of stellar irradiation in the second case.

Claims
Disc fragmentation is unlikely to produce giant planets around solar-type stars at radii <~50 AU. The disc does not fragment in both cases. The disc cannot cool fast enough in the first case. The disc is not gravitationally unstable in the second case. The cooling time is >~2tORB within ~30 AU. The Toomre parameter Q >~1.5 in the second case. The disc cools fast enough to fragment at radii >~20 AU in the second case. Fragmentation is possible at larger distances (>~100 AU). The findings have implications for understanding hot Jupiter formation. The findings corroborate previous work.
The results are consistent with previous simulations despite different radiative transfer treatments. The results are comparable with previous simulations. The agreement is reassuring. The temperatures are ~15% higher than Boley et al. (2006). The temperatures are <3% higher than Cai et al. (2007). The findings suggest that the conclusions are robust.

Data And Code Availability
The computations were performed using the UK Astrophysical Fluids Facility (UKAFF). The code dragon is used for the simulations. The code has been extensively tested.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The simulation was repeated using a smaller number of SPH particles (5 × 10^4). The evolution of the thermal energy, surface density, temperature, Toomre parameter and cooling time were essentially the same. The profiles change only slowly with time as the disc cools quasi-statically.

Ethical Considerations
The authors thank R. Durisen, A. Boley and K. Rice for useful discussions. The authors acknowledge support by PPARC grant PP/E000967/1.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the internal energy of the disc for both cases. Figure 2 shows the logarithmic column density and cross-section of the density. Figure 3 shows the logarithmic temperature in the x-y plane and on the x-z plane. Figure 4 shows the Toomre parameter in the x-y plane and on the x-z plane. Figure 5 shows the cooling time in the x-y plane and on the x-z plane. Figure 6 shows the surface density and temperature at 5 instances during the disc evolution. Figure 7 shows the Toomre parameter and cooling time at 5 instances during the disc evolution. Figure 8 shows the disc temperature profiles vertically to the disc midplane. Figure 9 shows the logarithmic column density and cross-section of the density for a disc heated by the central star. Figure 10 shows the logarithmic temperature in the x-y plane and on the x-z plane for a disc heated by the central star. Figure 11 shows the Toomre parameter in the x-y plane and on the x-z plane for a disc heated by the central star. Figure 12 shows the cooling time in the x-y plane and on the x-z plane for a disc heated by the central star.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is that disc fragmentation is unlikely to produce giant planets around solar-type stars at radii <~50 AU. 2. The strongest evidence is that the disc does not fragment in both cases due to cooling or stability constraints. 3. The future path is to investigate fragmentation at larger distances and its implications for planetary formation.

summary.title: Mechanochemical synthesis of eco-friendly fertilizer from eggshell (calcite) and KH2PO4
summary.authors: Roger Borges; Amanda Soares Giroto; Rodrigo Klaic; Fernando Wypych; Caue Ribeiro
summary.field_subfield: Materials chemistry / agricultural chemistry (reverse logistics, mechanochemistry, fertilizer science)
summary.type_of_paper: Experimental study (materials synthesis, characterization, and release kinetics)
summary.executive_summary: This study presents an environmentally beneficial and cost-effective method of producing calcium phosphate bioceramics (potassium calcium phosphates) for soil conditioning, based on reverse logistics and green chemistry. The method uses a free-solvent mechanochemical process between eggshell waste (calcite, CaCO3) and monobasic potassium dihydrogen phosphate (KH2PO4). The resulting K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4 phases provide better nutrient management of P, K, and Ca. When applied to soil, the material first releases K and forms hydroxyapatite, serving as an important bioavailable source of P and Ca at pH ~5, which comprises a large part of many countries' soils. Eggshells are important wastes of food industries and excellent CaCO3 sources (more specifically calcite), with everyday millions of tons produced as biowaste around the world, disposed in landfills with no pretreatment and producing odors due to microbial growth. The solid-state mechanochemical activation consists in applying mechanical energy to promote a chemical reaction from solid reagents using mainly friction and impact forces. The process mainly produces K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4, among other non-crystalline compounds and also CO2 resulting from CaCO3 decomposition. Compared to KH2PO4, all these phosphates may exhibit very different solubility according to the different bonds between different metal cations. The produced potassium calcium phosphates may be classified as smart release fertilizers, since they provide a delay of the bioavailability of P and K and also improve the bioavailability of Ca. The solid-state mechanochemical activation allows the reactions to occur in a solvent-free environment, producing no liquid or solid waste in the process. The literature reports the mechanochemical synthesis of hydroxyapatite from different precursors, but no mechanochemical process has been reported for the production of K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4 from calcite provided by eggshell and KH2PO4. The eggshells were collected by the authors in their homes, washed with water and dried at room temperature, presenting a diameter between 1 and 10 mm before the grinding process. The milling process was performed with a high-energy ball mill, Fritsch Pulverisette 7, with a 250 ml zirconia bowl, 5 zirconia balls of 15 mm diameter. The essays were performed using the weight ratio of 1:1 (w/w) of eggshell and KH2PO4 for various times and speeds. After milled, the samples were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD), nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) MAS, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). The nutrient content of the samples and precursors were obtained dissolving the samples by using acid digestion in H2SO4/H2O2 PA mixture (8:1 v/v, by 24 h at 250 °C), and determined by atomic absorption (K and Ca) and colorimetric (P) methods. The phosphorus diffusion rates in soil were performed in Petri dishes containing moist soil, according to the method described by Degryse and Mclaughlin (2014). The kinetic study of the nutrient release was firstly evaluated in citric acid solution (wt 2%) according to the recommended procedure from MAPA. The kinetic study of the nutrient release was also evaluated in soil. The produced potassium calcium phosphates may be classified as smart release fertilizers, since they provide a delay of the bioavailability of P and K and also improve the bioavailability of Ca. The solid-state mechanochemical activation allows the reactions to occur in a solvent-free environment, producing no liquid or solid waste in the process. The literature reports the mechanochemical synthesis of hydroxyapatite from different precursors, but no mechanochemical process has been reported for the production of K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4 from calcite provided by eggshell and KH2PO4. The kinetic study of the nutrient release was also evaluated in soil. The authors acknowledge support from CNPq, and thank the Agronano Network, the Agroenergy Laboratory, and the National Nanotechnology Laboratory for Agribusiness for providing institutional support and facilities.

Research Context
Reverse logistics is an instrument of economic and social development characterized by a set of actions, procedures and means to enable the collection and restitution of solid waste to the business sector, for reuse, in its cycle or in other cycles productive, or other environmentally appropriate final destination. An application of this concept is to provide novel processes for the synthesis of different calcium and / or potassium phosphates from any source of calcium carbonate (CaCO3), making it a soil conditioner. Among sources, eggshells are important wastes of food industries and excellent CaCO3 sources (more specifically calcite) (Byeon, 2016), with monobasic potassium dihydrogen phosphate. Everyday millions of tons of eggshells are produced as biowaste around the world, disposed in landfills with no pretreatment and producing odors due to microbial growth. Normally the reactions are processed by solid state mechanochemical activation, to produce different materials concerning physico-chemical features, especially the solubilization and diffusion of its constitutional elements and chemical species. Basically, the solid-state mechanochemical activation consists in applying mechanical energy to promote a chemical reaction (Kouznetsov et al., 2016) from solid reagents using mainly friction and impact forces. The process mechanism involved is still quite complex to evaluate, but the applied energy must be large enough to be able to break the reagent bonds and promote solid phase ion migration, in the case of this study, to form a new structure. The literature reports the mechanochemical synthesis of hydroxyapatite (Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2) from different precursors to those reported in this study (Chaikina et al., 2019), and even if from eggshell, the method uses phosphoric acid solution instead of powder phosphate salts (Francis and Rahman, 2016). Thus, as far as the authors know, no mechanochemical process has been reported for the production of calcium and potassium hydrogen phosphate (K3CaH(PO4)2) and potassium calcium phosphate (CaKPO4) from calcite provided by eggshell and KH2PO4, i.e. different structures from hydroxyapatite including potassium as one of the main components. It is in this sense that new technologies of ecological fertilizer production have been prioritizing environmental care using industrial and other potential wastes in the formulation of new products (Ivanov et al., 2019; Krishna et al., 2017; Santos et al., 2019; Cichy et al., 2019), avoiding unnecessary economic losses, are primarily relevant in the current socio-environmental scenario.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a free-solvent mechanochemical process between eggshell waste and KH2PO4 can produce new potassium calcium phosphate phases that improve nutrient management of P, K, and Ca in soil. The study hypothesizes that the produced potassium calcium phosphates may be classified as smart release fertilizers, since they provide a delay of the bioavailability of P and K and also improve the bioavailability of Ca. The study hypothesizes that these materials would promote better nutrient management by delaying the bioavailability of phosphorus and potassium (which are highly soluble from KH2PO4) and increasing the calcium bioavailability. The study hypothesizes that the new phosphates phases from milling made calcium readily available, an opposite effect to the delay observed for phosphorus and potassium. The study hypothesizes that the slower release for calcium and phosphorus for 2 h/600 rpm sample and the P radial diffusion are probably related to hydroxyapatite formation, identified from 3 until 30 days in soil conditions. The predicted outcome is that the material first releases K and forms hydroxyapatite, serving as an important bioavailable source of P and Ca at pH ~5, which comprises a large part of many countries' soils. The predicted outcome is that these materials would exhibit very different solubility according to the different bonds between different metal cations, influenced by the size of the metal cation and its charge, influencing the reticular energy of the structure.

The eggshells were collected by the authors in their homes, washed with water and dried at room temperature, presenting a diameter between 1 and 10 mm before the grinding process. The KH2PO4 PA was supplied from Vetec. The milling process was performed with high-energy ball mill, Fritsch Pulverisette 7, with a 250 ml zirconia bowl, 5 zirconia balls of 15 mm diameter. The essays were performed using the weight ratio of 1:1 (w/w) of eggshell and KH2PO4 were performed firstly for 15 min, 30 min, 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, 6 h, 12 h and 24 h at 600 rpm, and secondly at 100, 200, 400 and 600 rpm for 2 h. Considering the purity of KH2PO4 and assuming that the eggshells are mainly composed by CaCO3, the mixture corresponds to 0.75 mmol of KH2PO4 and 1 mmol of CaCO3. After milled, the samples were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD), nuclear magnetic resonance, magic-angle spinning (NMR) MAS, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). The nutrient content of the samples and precursors were obtained dissolving the samples by using acid digestion in H2SO4/H2O2 PA mixture (8:1 v/v, by 24 h at 250 °C), and determined by atomic absorption (K and Ca) and colorimetric (P) methods. Before release essays at citric acid solution (2 wt%), the material has been pelletized to simulated commercial products. The pellets were obtained in steel pelletizer applying the pressure of 5 bar, and the weight was standardized to 100 mg/L of P. One single pellet were used in each essay in triplicate, that was placed in 10 mL beaker, this small beaker was immersed into 300 mL of 2% citric acid solution in a 600 mL beaker, the system was kept closed with polyvinyl chloride (PVC) film, in a constant temperature room at 25 °C and under a magnetic stirring. The stirring ensures homogeneous distribution of diffused elements, and aliquots of 1.2 mL at different times (from 15 min to 30 days) have been collected to evaluate the release behavior and allow the calculation of a release kinetic model of Ca, K and P. This method consists to use a pre-treated paper to mark the P diffusion in soil. There is a direct relationship between the time and milling speed and the increasing of total energy involved. In general, it was noticed that only a minimal energy is required to initiate the mechanochemical reaction and, as a consequence, the diffraction patterns have huge changes attributed to the formation of different polymorphic potassium calcium phosphate phases. The TGA curve of KH2PO4 show two main loss events: since it is an anhydrous material, the moisture loss is not seen and the first step at 200°C should be associated to crystallization water loss. The second step at 300°C corresponds to polycondensation, concomitant with structural water loss. The residual mass (89%) regards to KPO3 formation is consistent to the theoretical (87%) (Fig. 2). summary.title: A Workflow for Identifying Viable Crystal Structures with Partially Occupied Sites Applied to Solid Electrolyte: Cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12

summary.field_subfield: Computational Materials Science / Solid-State Ionics
summary.executive_summary: Solid electrolytes are central to next-generation Li-ion batteries because they promise higher energy density, improved safety, longer lifetimes, and reduced production costs relative to liquid electrolytes. Among candidates, cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12 (c-LLZO) stands out for its excellent interfacial stability against metallic Li, but it is not stable at room temperature and is typically stabilised with substitutional dopants on the 24d sites. c-LLZO crystallises in the Ia 3d space group with Li atoms partially occupying the 24d and 96h sites, and there is no consensus on the correct Li occupancy ratio. Prior computational studies have relied on a single experimental occupancy as a starting point to build an idealised unit cell, which raises the concern that predicted structures may not be near the ground state and that derived thermodynamic and observable properties may be poorly described. This study introduces a combinatorial workflow that generates all possible Li site occupancies for a c-LLZO unit cell and orders them energetically. The authors first eliminate structures with overlapping Li atoms by imposing a minimal Li-Li distance of 1.7 Å, then remove symmetry-equivalent duplicates using local sensitive hashing (LSH) to reduce the configuration space from ~2.3 × 10 8 structures to ~2 × 10 6 symmetry-unique structures. They then fit a multiple linear regression (MLR) model trained on 1235 single-point DFT calculations performed with the ONETEP code (PBE functional, 830 eV kinetic energy cutoff) to energetically rank the remaining structures. The workflow finds that all structures occur within 5.8 eV of the lowest-energy structure, that 19 of the 20 lowest-energy structures have a 24d:96h ratio of 8:48, and that four structures within 0.026 eV (1 kT at 298 K) of the ground state share the same 24d configuration with only slight variations in the 96h configuration. The authors argue that a large proportion of previously reported experimental and theoretical structures may not be physically feasible or stable, and they provide all generated structures in a freely accessible database to improve accuracy and reproducibility. The paper is a preprint (ChemRxiv, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0) and does not report a formal bibliography, so top_influential_citations is empty. Notable omissions include the absence of author affiliations, participant demographics (not applicable to a computational study), and detailed hyperparameter reporting beyond the DFT settings.

Research Context
The motivation is that solid electrolytes offer higher energy density, improved safety, longer lifetimes, and reduced production costs versus liquid electrolytes. c-LLZO has the best interfacial stability of all popular fast ion conducting solid electrolytes against metallic Li. c-LLZO has two primary polymorphs, the highly conducting disordered cubic LLZO (c-LLZO) and ordered tetragonal LLZO (t-LLZO).

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central problem is that experimental and theoretical works have been unable to uncover the ground state configuration of c-LLZO.

Methodological Details
The study targets the crystallographically predicted structure of c-LLZO with a Hermann-Maguin space group of Ia 3d. c-LLZO has Li atoms partially occupying the 24d and 96h sites, which the authors use as the framework for generation. The authors neglect to include the 48g site that occurs between the 96h sites as it is not reported in most refinements. The total number of ways to populate 120 sites with 56 Li is 120 56 ≈ 7.4 × 10 34, rendering brute-force combinatorial search unviable. The authors eliminate overlapping Li atoms by imposing a minimal Li-Li distance of 1.7 Å. The chosen cutoff of 1.7 Å is less than 2 times the ionic radius of a Li atom and smaller than the minimum distance in t-LLZO (2.56 Å). Any minimal distance between 1.67 Å and 2.3 Å would be suitable for a numerical implementation. The geometric constraint limits 96h occupancy because each 96h site exists as a pair within 0.68 Å of each other. Each 24d occupation eliminates 4 out of 96h sites as they are within 1.67 Å of this site. The authors generate all possible structures using the crystal structure sites reported by Buschmann et al.

Procedures And Architectures
The authors generate all allowed structures by first generating all possible 24d permutations for a given 24d occupancy. The authors then populate the remaining 96h sites such that no two nearest neighbours are occupied simultaneously. The generation produces approximately 2.3 × 10 8 structures, including symmetry-equivalent duplicates. The authors construct the upper triangular connectivity matrix of the Li sub-lattice for each structure. The connectivity matrix is defined as the distances between each Li atom to every other Li atom. The matrix is then flattened and sorted to ensure uniformity in all matrices. The authors use local sensitive hashing (LSH) to perform fast approximate similarity searches. The use of LSH optimises the pairwise comparison from scaling at O(N 2 ) to O(N ). The symmetry comparison method allows symmetry checks on over 100 million structures in a reasonable time frame. Only approximately 1% of structures are symmetrically unique, allowing a reduction by a further factor of approximately 100. The reduced configuration space is around 2 × 10 6 structures, which the authors then energetically order. The authors perform DFT calculations on small subsets to fit a multiple linear regression (MLR) model.

Key Results
The authors performed 1235 single point DFT calculations in total. The DFT calculations were performed with the ONETEP code, which scales linearly with the number of atoms. The authors used the PBE GGA exchange correlation functional with a kinetic energy cutoff of 830 eV. The authors used a kinetic energy cutoff of 830 eV. The structures were represented by a frequency occurrence list of all possible Li-Li interactions. The data were split into test and training sets with a 1:3 ratio. The MLR model achieved a correlation of 0.9996 on the test set. All structures are found to occur within a range of 5.8 eV of our lowest energy structure. 19 out of the 20 lowest energy structures have a ratio of 8:48, with the 19th lowest being 9:47. The average energy for all structures occurs at 1.47 eV higher than the ground state structures. There are four structures, all 8:48, within 0.026 eV (1 kT at 298 K) of the lowest energy structure. The COMPASSIII forcefield ordered the 13:43 ratio with a correlation coefficient of 0.991.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The energetic preference to avoid 24d occupation is indicated by the average energy for each ratio increasing with increasing 24d occupancy. The four lowest energy structures have very similar atomic coordinates with only slight variations in the 96h configuration. The authors note that the energetic ordering procedure does not include entropic contributions and assumes reasonable retention of ordering upon geometry relaxation. The geometry optimisation results indicate that movement from original sites is preferable to attain lower energies. The authors conclude that a large proportion of experimental and theoretical literature predicts structures not reflective of a real system.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors acknowledge that the energetic ordering procedure does not include entropic contributions. The authors assume a reasonable retention of ordering upon geometry relaxation, which is an approximation. The authors have tested the effect of geometry relaxation on a small dataset of 20 structures. A large-scale energy prediction of the geometry optimised structures falls outside the scope of this communication. The authors note that the Coulombic forces alone are not sufficient to energetically order c-LLZO structures. The authors acknowledge that the trade-off for increased speed and lower memory costs is the high specificity of the LSH method. The authors acknowledge that the COMPASSIII issue was considered too large to surmount in this paper. The authors neglect to include the 48g site, which may limit the completeness of the generated structures. The paper is a preprint not peer-reviewed by ChemRxiv, which may limit its reliability.
